The Best Tech Gifts for Design Enthusiasts

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it.
  • For this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do.
  • The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

For this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with upcoming technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store.

The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Studebaker’s retro-inspired design brings the 1980s into the present with Bluetooth connectivity, a CD player, USB playback, and a cassette deck that can even record music. A rechargeable battery and built-in carrying handle make it easy to take the nostalgia wherever the party goes.

The SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox is available at store.moma.org for $250.

Photography courtesy of Polaroid.

Polaroid’s Mod puts creative controls directly on the camera, inviting experimentation without the distraction of a smartphone screen. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

Photography courtesy of Therabody.

In a recent development, therabody takes a different approach to workout recovery with a device designed to fit between your hands. To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

The CryoTherm Palm is available at therabody.com for $399.99.

Photography courtesy of Balmuda.

Inspired by traditional pocket watches, Balmuda’s The Clock reimagines how we experience time through light, sound, and movement. Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Clock is available at us.balmuda.com for $499 in Silver and $519 in Champagne.

Photography courtesy of Bang & Olufsen.

Industry observers note that bang & Olufsen’s Beoplay H100 headphones are undeniably a splurge, but they’re designed with longevity in mind. The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. It’s an investment piece for someone who appreciates exceptional craftsmanship as much as great audio.

The Beoplay H100 Headphones are available at bang-olufsen.com for $2,200.

Photography courtesy of Warby Parker.

Smart glasses are getting a stylish upgrade thanks to Warby Parker’s collaboration with Google and Samsung. Available in three of the brand’s familiar silhouettes, the lightweight frames incorporate a camera, open-ear speakers, and Gemini AI for hands-free photography, calls, navigation, and more. Subtly translucent temples offer a glimpse of the technology inside without compromising the classic eyewear design. With prescription, nonprescription, reading, and sunglass options, they’re a surprisingly versatile gift.

Intelligent Eyewear is available for preorder at warbyparker.com, starting at $395.

Photography courtesy of Flowtica.

What looks like an ordinary ballpoint pen has a few technological tricks up its sleeve. The Flowtica Scribe combines a functional writing instrument with an AI-powered voice recorder, allowing owners to capture conversations while taking notes on paper the old-fashioned way. A companion app can transcribe recordings and turn them into summaries and action items, bringing digital convenience to a familiar analog tool. An optional vegan leather charging case gives the device a place to rest between meetings.

The Flowtica Scribe is available at flowtica.ai for $159.

Photography courtesy of Bellroy.

According to recent reports, anyone who’s ever untangled a mess of charging cables at the bottom of a bag will appreciate Bellroy’s thoughtfully designed Tech Kit. The small organizer opens flat to reveal a series of mesh pockets and elastic loops that keep chargers, cables, earbuds, and other tech essentials neatly in place. Its structured shape makes everything easy to see and access, while the streamlined exterior, made from recycled woven fabric, slips neatly into a backpack or carry-on. It’s a simple solution to one of travel’s most persistent little annoyances.

The Tech Kit is available at bellroy.com for $59–$69, depending on color.

It has been revealed that amazon’s latest Kindle redesign brings a more refined look and feel to the familiar e-reader. The Paperwhite Signature Edition pairs a sleek aluminum body with a 7-inch, glare-free display, adjustable warm lighting, and double-tap page turning. Waterproof construction and wireless charging make it an easy travel companion, while two finishes, Graphite and Seaglass Green, offer a choice between classic and colorful.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is available at amazon.com for $250.

Photography courtesy of Daily Objects.

In a recent development, who claims charging stations have to be boring? DailyObjects’ Surge Foldaway turns an everyday tech essential into a sculptural desktop accessory. Its adjustable design accommodates an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, consolidating three charging spots into one tidy footprint. The bold Cosmic Orange finish adds a welcome pop of color, giving the accessory a presence even when the devices are elsewhere.

The Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger is available at dailyobjects.us for $175.

Photography courtesy of ModRetro.

Recent findings suggest that A love letter to handheld gaming, ModRetro’s Chromatic brings the original Game Boy experience into the present with a few thoughtful upgrades. Its magnesium-alloy body houses a custom, pixel-perfect display designed to play original Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges. The colorful finishes include four translucent options that expose the internal hardware, turning the console’s components into part of its visual identity.

The Chromatic + Tetris Bundle is available at modretro.com starting at $199.

According to recent reports, shark’s CryoGlow Plus combines two skincare technologies in a single wearable device: LED light therapy and under-eye cooling. Red, blue, and infrared lights power several treatment modes, while adjustable cooling pads help refresh tired eyes. The upgraded design offers improved LED coverage around the eyes and mouth, and the soft Pastel Berry finish makes this wearable gadget surprisingly stylish.

The CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask is available at sharkninja.com for $379.99.

In a market crowded with phones competing for attention, the Mudita Kompakt is designed to demand less of it. Its minimalist design centers on a 4.3-inch E Ink display, favoring a restrained interface over colorful notifications and app-heavy screens. Essential features like calling, messaging, offline maps, and a camera remain, while a dedicated offline switch offers a physical way to disconnect.

The Mudita Kompakt is available at mudita.com for $399.

According to recent reports, who notes smart technology has to look high-tech? Birdfy’s Feeder Wood combines the charm of a traditional wooden birdhouse with a built-in camera, letting bird lovers watch their feathered visitors up close. Made from FSC-certified wood, the solar-powered feeder captures 1080p video. Its companion app can identify more than 6,000 bird species, bringing a layer of digital discovery to an otherwise familiar backyard ritual.

The Feeder Wood is available at birdfy.com for $189.99.

Wallie’s approach to the digital photo frame starts with a simple idea: make the screen look less like a screen. Its 10-inch color E Ink display gives photographs the appearance of printed images, while real wood construction and a choice of four finishes help it blend into a gallery wall or shelf arrangement. Rounded or square corners offer further customization, and a rechargeable battery eliminates the need for a visible power cord. Photos can be updated remotely through an app.

The Wallie 10 is available at shop.wallieframe.com for $299.

With its simple spherical form, Eve Flare looks more like an illuminated object than a conventional lamp. The rechargeable, water-resistant light offers millions of customizable colors, with app and voice controls for setting the mood indoors or outside. Its wireless charging base and portable design mean it can move effortlessly from a bedside table to the patio, adding a little atmosphere wherever it lands.

The Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp is available at apple.com for $99.95.

Photography courtesy of Best Buy.

According to recent reports, 8BitDo borrows the visual language of the original Nintendo Entertainment System for a mechanical keyboard that feels straight out of the 1980s. Chunky gray keys, red accents, and tactile mechanical switches establish the retro aesthetic, while an included joystick and two oversized programmable buttons bring arcade-style controls to the desktop. Bluetooth and wireless connectivity keep the throwback design compatible with contemporary setups.

The 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition is available at bestbuy.com for $79.99.

Photography courtesy of Orbitkey.

Industry observers note that even the most organized desk tends to accumulate charging cables, adapters, and other small tech accessories. Orbitkey’s Nest v2 gives them a designated home in a compact storage box with adjustable dividers and a fabric-lined interior. The removable leather-covered lid doubles as a valet tray and 15W wireless charger, keeping everyday essentials within reach while concealing the clutter underneath.

The Nest v2 is available at orbitkey.com for $125.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.
  • In a recent development, “By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

In a recent development, “By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” states a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

Industry observers note that the calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

According to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735).

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

Meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, claims in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”.

OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the new Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

According to recent reports, the architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” claims Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Industry observers note that inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

In the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

According to recent reports, the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into new objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

It has been revealed that designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

Sources indicate that “We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving fresh value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

In a recent development, at the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

Murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.

According to recent reports, naming is hard. The language we use shapes the way we think about things, but also the conversation we have about it. That’s why we have so much confusion about colors, icons, UI components, features — and that’s why we struggle to name design tokens, HTML classes, and variables.

Sometimes, the names we choose are too generic, so it’s difficult to understand what exactly is meant. And sometimes they are too specific, leaving little room for flexibility and reuse. How do we choose the right names? And which naming conventions work best? Let’s take a closer look.

If you’re looking for some inspiration for naming HTML classes, CSS properties, or JavaScript functions, Classnames is a wonderful resource jam-packed with ideas that get you thinking outside the box.

It has been revealed that the site provides thematically grouped lists of words perfect for naming. You’ll find terms to describe different kinds of behavior, likeness between things, order, grouping, and association, but also themed collections of words that wouldn’t instantly come to one’s mind when it comes to code, among them words from nature, art, theater, music, architecture, fashion, and publishing.

According to recent reports, how would you choose the right name for a given color? Fortunately, David Aerne maintains a tremendous repository of color names, currently with 30355 unique color names, sourced from various references and 1000s of user contributions.

According to recent reports, of course, the repository comes with a color picker and name search and plenty of other color pickers as well. Tremendous work, which is also a fantastic reference to keep nearby.

Industry observers note that what makes a good name? Javier Cuello summarized a set of naming best practices that help you name your layers, groups, and components in a consistent and scalable way.

As Javier points out, a good name has a logical structure, is short, meaningful, known by everyone, and not related to visual properties. He shares do’s and don’ts to illustrate how to achieve that and also takes a closer look at all the fine little details you need to consider when naming sizes, colors, groups, layers, and components.

Recent findings suggest that how to build a flexible design token taxonomy that works across different products? That was the challenge that the team at Intuit faced. The parent tech giant of products such as Mailchimp, QuickBooks, TurboTax, and Mint developed a flexible token system that goes beyond the brand theme to serve as the foundational system for a wide array of products.

Nate Baldwin wrote a case study in which he shares valuable insights into the making of Intuit’s design token taxonomy. It dives deeper into the pain points of the old taxonomy system, the criteria they defined for the new system, and how it was created. Lots of takeaways for building your own robust and flexible token taxonomy are guaranteed.

Looking at what other people call similar things is a great way to start when you’re struggling with naming. And what better source could there be than other design systems? Before you end up in the design system rabbit hole, Iain Bean did the research for you and created the Component Gallery.

It has been revealed that it’s a collection that includes plenty of examples for more than 50 UI components — from accordion to visually hidden — and also lists other names that the UI components go by. A fantastic resource, and not only with regard to naming.

Features often have low adoption due to poor discoverability. Feature adoption needs time — first the feature must be discovered, then understood, then tried, learned, and eventually built into existing workflow. Erin Gannon has written a helpful practical guide on how to make sure all of it happens.

Good names are driven by user needs and problems. They should signal the value or outcome of a feature (the job-to-be-done), and — most importantly! — tap into the user’s own language. So ask people to explain a feature in their own words and then use the words they use.

A wonderful example of naming guidelines for a complex multi-brand, multi-themed design system comes from the Vodafone UK Design System team. Their Variables Taxonomy Map breaks down the anatomy and categorization of a design token into a well-orchestrated system of collections.

The map illustrates four collections required to support the system and connections between tokens — from brand and primitives to semantics and pages. It builds on top of Nathan Curtis’ work on naming design tokens and enables everyone to gather insight about where a token is used and what it represents, just from its name.

If you want to explore more approaches to naming design tokens, I’ve put together a list of useful Figma kits and resources that are worth checking out.

Romina Kavcic created a helpful little tool for naming design tokens — from learning how they work and how to name them well to configuring your own naming structure with components, categories, states, and roles.

If you are looking for the right name for your product or service, Onym is a fantastic open-source repository that organizes tools and resources for finding names for brainstorming, vetting, guides, sprints, etymologies — all the way to cautionary tales and agencies that name things, as well as useful books to take a look at.

A quick-reference list of tools and guides for naming just about… well, anything, in one place:.

Recent findings suggest that the right name is the one that’s well-understood and used by the team and owners. So much time is wasted speaking about the very same thing but in different dialects — the designer’s dialect, the developer’s dialect, the product manager’s dialect, and the user’s dialect. That’s what often causes frustration and confusion.

So if you see low adoption, it might be merely because of the name. And pay attention to potential naming conflicts and put them in a backlog of things to address later. It’s one of those fine little details that can reduce frustration and confusion and help teams work together better.

We hope you’ll find these wonderful projects useful — put together by wonderful creators. A friendly shout-out to everyone sharing their work with folks to use and learn from! That’s one of the reasons why we truly love the web and people building and designing it. 💚.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City.
  • Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date.
  • In a recent development, the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a fresh way to move between them.

In a recent development, the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

Recent findings suggest that “People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”.

According to recent reports, the installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

In a recent development, twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A new 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

Art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a fresh location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

Sources indicate that for SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he notes. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”.

Sources indicate that the expansion also introduces more than 80 fresh retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

Yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

The latest public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

Tiffany & Co. Brings a Century of American Beauty to Crystal Bridges

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co.
  • Discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co.
  • In a recent development, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the company’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

An 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the company’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Recent findings suggest that bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

Recent findings suggest that installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Recent findings suggest that “This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” says Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”.

Recent findings suggest that inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

George Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Sources indicate that the brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

George Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s New Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

Industry observers note that A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

While Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Industry observers note that jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Recent findings suggest that schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the firm’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”.

Jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Industry observers note that hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination is on view through Mar. 29, 2027, at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

#137437. Tech Report: Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2057 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Sources indicate that back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

Sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

Industry observers note that back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

The same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses manufacturer-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these new systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

Industry observers note that after all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

Recent findings suggest that the main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

Recent findings suggest that one strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more promptly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

But, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Sources indicate that also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a new tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

Sources indicate that that doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

Sources indicate that at a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

They need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

But formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff indicated their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a major downside… mistakes will be made.

Many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a new tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

It has been revealed that I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

It has been revealed that what they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

Sources indicate that this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Sources indicate that look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

In a recent development, staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

Recent findings suggest that but too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

That mentioned, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

Again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

Industry observers note that today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

It has been revealed that take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are right now bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

And that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

That is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Firm data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

Industry observers note that the instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it demonstrates exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Industry observers note that organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

Industry observers note that I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out upcoming technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.

With practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A.

In a recent development, everything TypeScript, with code walkthroughs and examples. And other printed books.

#137436. Newly introduced bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

Newly introduced bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed?
  • In a recent development, juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence.
  • Industry observers note that though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a latest bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.

In a recent development, juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).

Industry observers note that though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.

Sources indicate that “On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.

According to recent reports, central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo states, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”.

Detail of Justin Favela's Mantecore (White Tiger) (2017), featured in Qué tanto es tantito, a group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

It has been revealed that sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, introduced in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is currently in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.

It has been revealed that “A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”.

In a recent development, the Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” claims Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.

In a recent development, sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.

According to recent reports, “There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” says Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”.

Installation view of the group show Costuras Territoriales at the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso Courtesy of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso.

In El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra notes. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”.

It has been revealed that independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” claims Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.

Installation view ofthe group exhibiton Qué tanto es tantito, group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso.

In a recent development, sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.

Sources indicate that picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other challenges. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.

Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo claims. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”.

Industry News: How to Start a Side Business While Working Full-Time

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • It has been revealed that the number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy.
  • Validation does not require a perfect product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

It has been revealed that the number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you initiative to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

Industry observers note that the FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Industry observers note that forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

It has been revealed that side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Company). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

It has been revealed that an LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

According to recent reports, self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Recent findings suggest that deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

Ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

It has been revealed that side hustlers! With the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card you can earn free travel from your business expenses.

ChooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

It has been revealed that the biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

The 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

In a recent development, the FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

According to recent reports, but here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the notable thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Sources indicate that talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

In a recent development, pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

According to recent reports, open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

In a recent development, pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Industry observers note that check your employment contract and organization handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Recent findings suggest that most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

It has been revealed that businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Industry observers note that start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Recent findings suggest that dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function
