Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.
  • The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.
  • Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.

The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.

Leisure and wellness projects win big again.

The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.

“It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added.

The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.

Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico.

A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning architecture projects below:.

Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi.

The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly.

The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

“Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” remarked the master jury.

“It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.”.

House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects.

Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast.

This house demonstrates how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature.

The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.

“This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury said.

“In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.”.

House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office.

Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China.

This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result.

The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

“This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” said the judges.

“Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.”.

Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos.

Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.

A deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core.

Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.

The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”.

According to recent reports, “It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they said.

Recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo.

Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability.

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.

The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.

“It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.

House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects.

Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran.

It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life.

Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.”.

“It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they mentioned.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture.

French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves.

The new building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

“A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” stated the master jury.

“It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.”.

Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture.

Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States.

A very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner.

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.

The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”.

“It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added.

Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects.

Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.

The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.

The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

“A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.

“The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.”.

Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works.

Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

Well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour.

The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects.

Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India.

In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most latest constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould.

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people.

“This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury.

“In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most latest constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.

“The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects.

French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France.

It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant.

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a latest purpose.

“It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” noted the judges.

“The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.”.

Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects.

Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson.

There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint.

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.

The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.

“There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they stated.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT.

Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.

A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train.

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a fresh public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.”.

It has been revealed that “A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.”.

Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects.

Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

A minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way.

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”.

Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu.

Architecture studio Tonkin Liu won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in York, United Kingdom.

The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space.

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral.

“There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure,” said the judges.

“The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a latest generation of makers using the space,” they added.

Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733.

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

Despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals’ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The judges praised the project as “rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists,” adding that, “despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.”.

Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio.

Rammed Earth house by Tuckey Design Studio in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year, sponsored by Michelmersh.

Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe.

Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.

As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as “a radical example of material innovation”.

“Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe,” they noted.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo.

Dutch firm Mecanoo won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank in Amsterdam.

An admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building.

The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

The renovation was praised as “an admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building,” by the master jury, who also noted its efforts to adapt it to a different use “while also addressing material and energy concerns.”.

Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Breaking: Discover this year's Dezeen Awards Designers of the Year

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dezeen has unveiled the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.
  • Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.
  • This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dezeen has unveiled the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.

Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.

Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.

London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.

Read more about the Designers of the Year below:.

Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet.

Architect of the year: Lina Ghotmeh.

Sources indicate that ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.

“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” noted the judges.

“Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”.

Ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.

Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.

Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo.

Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” said the judges.

“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”.

Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.

His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.

Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa.

Recent findings suggest that interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” said the judges.

“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”.

Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.

Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.

Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem.

Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.

“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” said the judges.

“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”.

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.

Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.

Designer of the year: Yinka Ilori.

Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.

“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” mentioned the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”.

Recent findings suggest that ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.

He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.

Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language.

Emerging designer of the year: Simon Skinner.

Swedish designer Skinner is well-known for his furniture, sculpture and installations that explore how materials can be rethought or reused.

According to recent reports, “Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language. His work subverts the familiar, creating distinct new objects that hint at an exciting new direction for design.”.

Recent examples of his varied, multidisciplinary work include a range of sculptural lights made from second-hand bowls, ashtrays and cat figurines.

#137371. Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1423 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • India’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
  • Recent findings suggest that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for massive works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
  • For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

India’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers said that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

Recent findings suggest that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for massive works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

For India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” stated Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a newly introduced buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

In the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

According to recent reports, subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” noted the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

With India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox remarked this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

Also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that demonstrated at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (New York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

Several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read remarked that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

By and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which showed small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

While both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

Another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff said she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

Sources indicate that the gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff remarked.

Speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery demonstrated a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he said.

The gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

As many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," says the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

Recent findings suggest that further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan noted, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

It has been revealed that meanwhile, concerns of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

India's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of new Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

Every copy of Accidental Collage arrives damaged on purpose. Created by Manchester studio Dr.Me and published by Waiting Room Press, the 400-page volume documents weathered billboard strata pulled from city walls. According to Itâs Nice That, Dr.Meâs Mark âEddyâ Edwards drew the cover idea from book artist Lydia Davies, who purposefully defiled the edges of her poetry books. That choice hits before the spine even opens. On the cover, bold sans-serif capitals stack vertically down the right edge, sliced diagonally by a physical paper tear: black letters sit on creased white stock above the rip, flipping to white ink over raw ochre pasteboard and red scraps underneath. It doesnât observe street decay from a polite distance. The book behaves like a city hoarding itself.

Inside, the book design drops white margins completely. Full-bleed photographs push straight to the trim edges, anchored only by tiny centered folios along the bottom border so nothing interrupts the torn paper layers. Thereâs no border competing for attention, so cross-gutter pairings drive the pace. On pages 74 and 75, two ripped portraits lock eyes across the fold â a face peeking through jagged olive-green stenciled stock opposite a monochrome eye buried under white shreds and a red slash. Turn to page 259 and red lips above torn yellow ribbons face giant blue halftone teeth bordered by an exposed CMYK color bar. Elsewhere, pages 312 and 313 pair a shredded magenta portrait and clipped white serif type against a violet sheet torn across the middle to reveal a mouth and ghosted lettering.

Edwards told Itâs Nice That the archive grew after lockdowns as a community began trading found dÃ©collages from Manhattan building hoardings, Parisian metro walls, and London Underground theatre posters. Interviews and essays by Sarah Boris, Nick Deakin, Braulio Amado, and experimental drummers Hisham Akira Bharoocha and Jeremy Gustin sit alongside the plates, linking ripped street bills to rhythm and print culture. On pages 354 and 355, a shredded gig poster dated 09.11.24 faces bold white ON A MISSION FOREVER lettering ripping open over yellow underlayers. Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (452 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.
  • Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.
  • “The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Salva López.

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”.

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides users away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” remarked Serra.

Serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra remarked.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

Photography by Salva López.

Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December.
  • In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair?
  • “We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” indicates misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” indicates misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

In a recent development, the campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

In a recent development, for soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

Industry observers note that and yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

According to recent reports, “Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

In a recent development, according to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

According to recent reports, ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch notes the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

In a recent development, “Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch says. She aims to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

According to recent reports, the “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

According to recent reports, as of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto claims, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

Sources indicate that for the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto indicates, “that would be a huge victory.”.

#137362. Tech Report: Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility.
  • The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol.
  • Recent findings suggest that that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a latest reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”.

Recent findings suggest that that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”.

It has been revealed that but is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

It has been revealed that our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a substantial deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Sources indicate that separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson claims. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”.

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”.

In a recent development, as with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson says. It’s also extra notable to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she indicates—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

#137359. Breaking: Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

📅 14 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1103 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone.
  • Industry observers note that it’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body.
  • Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

Industry observers note that it’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Sources indicate that mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next massive thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”.

The medication is right now in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide customers lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

It has been revealed that in fact, this has become such an matter that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”.

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”.

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

Recent findings suggest that but compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

In a recent development, but, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

In a recent development, dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

In a recent development, “Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel notes. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali claims. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more notable, he points out.

Giga rebuilds AD Italia for its 45th anniversary: the AD Italia redesign pairs Arizona type, Ghirri colour and a modernist grid.

The first thing you see is the masthead. AD sits in black flared serif on a soft pink field, the letters drawn wide enough to carry the cover on their own, and the same confidence runs through the issue. Inside, the November pages open on a white field with SPAZI set large in the same face, issue N.530, and the spreads that follow give each photograph a full page of air. The palette stays soft and everyday: coral, pale green and pale blue, the colours of an Italian landscape rather than a brand manual.

Sources indicate that proportion went to the type. Arizona, by Dinamo Typefaces, is almost a sans with flared strokes, and it brings the measure of Roman inscriptions to the page. A specimen page sets names in Arizona Flare Light, one per line, with nothing else on the field, and the same face carries the cover lines: SPAZI across a white cover, LA NOSTRA GUIDA AL SALONE 2025 stacked in white on black. The letters do the talking, and the layout stays out of their way.

Industry observers note that essentiality went to the grid. Giga built it on the logic of modern art catalogues: photographs get room of their own, captions stay small and precise, and the editorial pages stand apart from the advertising around them. A spread on David Bowie runs green panels beside a column of text that starts in 1972, when Bowie became Ziggy Stardust, and a grid of anniversary spreads collects 45 icons from the magazine's history on a single page.

In a recent development, colour went to Luigi Ghirri. The case page sets the palette beside three everyday Italian landscapes, a canal road, green houses against the sea, a beach with swings, all in the soft register of Ghirri's photographs. The system names its colours plainly: PMS 2344 C coral, PMS 2260 C pale green, PMS 290 C pale blue, each with its hex code printed beside it, the way a printer would want it.

According to recent reports, wit went to the rhythm. Like Ettore Sottsass's Carlton bookcase, which slants its shelves and still holds books, the system plays with its own conventions, varying titles and images from story to story. The redesign launched with the November 2026 issue and a room at PAC Milano built around one line: perfect proportions, essential function, a joke, the colours of every day.

Black timber elements traverse concrete fragrance store in Tokyo

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.
  • Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.
  • The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Takuya Yamauchi.

Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.

The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.

“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a new perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.

“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”.

Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.

Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.

Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.

“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” mentioned Esrawe.

“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.

“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”.

Recent findings suggest that xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.

Photography by Takuya Yamauchi.

Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record.
  • In a recent development, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates.
  • In a recent development, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

In a recent development, but the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in Latest York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

In a recent development, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s announced that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

According to recent reports, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's.

Estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Acquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

Soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s Fresh York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

In a recent development, the top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's.

According to recent reports, one of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

It has been revealed that mary Cassatt also established a new auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • pen.dev pairs a 60fps WebGL canvas and live shaders with browser import and two-way MCP integration for real product design.
  • Industry observers note that we've been testing pen.dev closely for quite some time, and we're ready to say it: for our daily work at Abduzeedo, it has gotten our full attention and replaced Figma in our day-to-day flow.
