#137317. Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Upcoming York

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1665 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Christie’s tepid 21st-century sale caps week of blockbuster auctions in Upcoming York

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees).
  • Sources indicate that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in New York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Sources indicate that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

In a recent development, another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

It has been revealed that price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a upcoming home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

Recent findings suggest that A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of notable 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Sources indicate that gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in New York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in Fresh York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a latest auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

In a recent development, though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime Latest York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Industry observers note that among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and notable champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Industry observers note that the evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the New York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Industry observers note that apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca noted. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

Tech Report: This Photographer Built a DIY Digital Rangefinder Using Two Old Canon Cameras

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that earlier this year, photographer and creator Mr.
  • Unlike the Micro Four Thirds-based camera Mr.
  • The Canon EOS M features an 18-megapixel APS-C CMOS image sensor, up from the 12.1-megapixel Micro Four Thirds sensor Mr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that earlier this year, photographer and creator Mr. 50mm built a DIY digital rangefinder camera using parts he salvaged from a FED 5 Soviet-era rangefinder and a Panasonic GF3 Micro Four Thirds camera. Mr. 50mm is back with an even better DIY digital rangefinder, and this time it’s APS-C.

Unlike the Micro Four Thirds-based camera Mr. 50mm dubbed the “RGM-79” earlier this year, the upcoming “C7M” uses a larger APS-C image sensor. Mr. 50mm is using the imaging pipeline from the original Canon EOS M mirrorless camera, which Canon unveiled way back in 2012.

The Canon EOS M features an 18-megapixel APS-C CMOS image sensor, up from the 12.1-megapixel Micro Four Thirds sensor Mr. 50mm salvaged from a Panasonic GF3.

In a recent development, A DIY digital rangefinder requires two donors, though. Rather than the FED 5 rangefinder Mr. 50mm used before, he’s sticking with two Canon cameras this time around. The donor rangefinder is the Canon 7, a rangefinder series that started in 1961 with the original Canon 7 and ended in 1967 with the Canon 7sZ.

Although Mr. 50mm hasn’t finalized everything or released a build video yet — it’s in the works — the C7M sure does look impressive thus far. Mr. 50mm is especially impressed with the Canon 7’s finder, which he describes as a “marked upgrade compared to a Fed camera.”.

“The bar wasn’t that high, but the Canon 7 does a lot of things very, very well. You get a brighter finder, you get projected and selectable frame lines, and they’re parallax-corrected,” the builder explains.

Further, the Canon 7 uses a Leica M39 screw mount, which is great news for Mr. 50mm. It’s a widely used mount with a ton of lens options on the market.

Sources indicate that while the Canon 7 doesn’t have many controls, that isn’t a downside for Mr. 50mm.

Sources indicate that “It doesn’t have that many dedicated controls, which helps reduce the amount of controls I need to either port or figure out if I’m okay to live without. In the end, the digital camera really just has to be able to do two things. It has to accommodate the rangefinder that I’m gonna put on top, and it has to be able to accommodate the mount that I’m using,” he explains.

There are plenty of challenges, though.

“Unfortunately, it isn’t just as easy as disassembling an EOS M and then jamming on newly introduced parts,” Mr. 50mm explains. “There [were] quite a few modifications that needed to be done to the camera to make this work, which I’ll discuss probably in depth in another video.”.

Ultimately, as the video above shows, he solved the biggest challenges. He says the C7M is “mostly done” and, impressively, it only took a couple of weeks to build from start to finish. Despite a damaging drop during the build, it came together pretty well.

Sources indicate that there’s always a catch, though. There are some rangefinder calibration issues left to figure out, and not everything aligns perfectly yet. Mr. 50mm indicates he needs to trim back some more material from the EOS M’s parts, although he isn’t sure how much they have left to give.

“Eventually, once things get a bit more ironed out, I’ll draft up a tutorial on how you can actually make your own,” the photographer notes.

So while the C7M isn’t totally finished yet, it looks very cool and even more promising. Digital rangefinder cameras are expensive, but building one using donor parts and 3D-printed components makes the format significantly more accessible, assuming someone is comfortable with the build process itself.

Sources indicate that although there isn’t a build tutorial yet, it’s still worth considering the potential cost to build a C7M. The Canon EOS M body is around $260 used, not much more than a Canon 7 rangefinder body. If someone has access to a 3D printer, printing the other parts won’t cost much. That’s much less than a brand-upcoming Leica digital rangefinder, for sure.

Canon EOS MBuy used on KEH.comCanon 7Buy used on KEH.com.

Keep an eye on Mr. 50mm’s (excellent) YouTube channel to stay up to date with the project.

#137315. I Couldn’t Imagine Working With a Photo Editor on a Different Continent

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (603 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

I Couldn’t Imagine Working With a Photo Editor on a Different Continent

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before I worked on the PetaPixel news desk, I was an agency photographer covering breaking news, features, and sports.
  • In a recent development, I was young and in need of guidance.
  • I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before I worked on the PetaPixel news desk, I was an agency photographer covering breaking news, features, and sports.

In a recent development, I was young and in need of guidance. I found that in the form of my photo editor, whom I’m going to call Gary.

I would speak to Gary every morning when he assigned me jobs for the day, talking me through what was expected and the specific set of photos I needed to produce.

After I wired him the photos, he would let me know whether I had done a good job or a terrible one.

He would often edit my photos, reframe them slightly, change the crop, cull some of them, or call me up and ask if I had a different angle.

But Gary did far more than that. He was a leader in the newsroom, worked closely with the news editor to shape stories and come up with ideas, and was an excellent salesman.

His vivacious personality helped. He invented nicknames for me and the other photographers, made silly jokes, and was just generally good for staff morale. Not everyone liked the owners, but everyone liked Gary.

Recent findings suggest that after I had worked there for a few years, the agency was bought out, and Gary moved to a new hub hundreds of miles away. Our relationship was never the same. The new regime was different, and I left soon after.

I thought of Gary this week when the Associated Press officially cut all eight of the remaining photo editor positions in the U.S.

Sources indicate that AP has moved the positions to its hub in Noida, India. The agency notes it has prepares to grow the Indian operation to 100 staff members, including video producers.

AP photo editors are legendary: Consider the famous Napalm Girl photograph, for example, when Horst Faas and Hal Buell overruled Carl Robinson’s decision not to wire Nick Ut’s photograph.

Photo editors have played a crucial role in the fortunes of photographers for a very long time, advocating for us while seeing the bigger picture.

It’s not a question of whether talented photo editors exist in India. Of course, they do. But there’s something valuable about having an editor who understands the local news environment, knows the photographers personally, and can build relationships over years of working together.

Recent findings suggest that and look, I get it: the press industry is tough. Agency bosses were once raking in vast sums of money — these days they face lousy picture rates from a fractured industry.

According to recent reports, photo editors do not attend a news story in person the way photographers do; therefore, they could theoretically be anywhere. This is a globalized, technologized world: workers in developing countries are technically in competition with workers from the U.S.

But while these major decisions make sense from a financial point of view, what are the long-term consequences?

Photographers, like my younger self, have fewer opportunities to benefit from a leading light like Gary.

According to recent reports, nowadays, photographers are increasingly expected to be fully formed; the bosses need someone they can rely on to do a good job no matter what. And while there are plenty of great photographers out there who can do that, they all had to cut their teeth somewhere.

As with many other things in life, it feels like the ladder for the younger generation is being removed.

#137312. Between Moonlight and Aurora: Photographing East Greenland After Dark

Between Moonlight and Aurora: Photographing East Greenland After Dark

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photographing East Greenland at night is an exercise in preparation, observation, and adaptation.
  • During a recent photography expedition in East Greenland, hosted by Secret Atlas this last October 2026, I spent several evenings leading the photographic project targeting enormous icebergs illuminated by the rising moon, alongside the Northern Lights appearing above the surrounding fjords and ice.
  • Some photographs begin long before the camera is taken out of the bag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photographing East Greenland at night is an exercise in preparation, observation, and adaptation. The landscape is immense, the conditions can be demanding, and the opportunities to make a particular image may be limited to a few minutes. Towering icebergs, drifting sea ice, fog, low clouds, and the changing Arctic sky create an environment in which light can completely transform the way a scene is perceived. Yet having spectacular scenery in front of you does not necessarily mean you will come away with a strong photograph. The challenge is to recognize what makes a moment worth capturing, understand how the available light interacts with the landscape, and make the right decisions before that moment disappears.

During a recent photography expedition in East Greenland, hosted by Secret Atlas this last October 2026, I spent several evenings leading the photographic project targeting enormous icebergs illuminated by the rising moon, alongside the Northern Lights appearing above the surrounding fjords and ice. These two subjects offered very different photographic challenges and a particular one-of-a-kind night operation.

Some photographs begin long before the camera is taken out of the bag. The moonrise series was one of those projects. Across four days, I followed the changing opportunities to photograph the rising moon among the enormous icebergs of East Greenland. The objective was not simply to record the moon above the horizon, but to find a relationship between the moonlight, the architecture of the icebergs, the sense of exploration, and the surrounding landscape.

The first opportunity to photograph the sequence came around 8 p.m. on day three of our expedition, when the timing and the available light finally began to align. In the Arctic, twilight can retain considerable ambient light even as the moon rises. This transition creates an interesting balance: the landscape may still hold detail, while the moon begins illuminating the ice from a different angle.

A rising moon and a monumental iceberg are impressive subjects individually, but putting them together is not enough. Their positions, relative sizes, illumination, and separation from the background all influence how the image is read. Anticipating these relationships is essential, particularly when the window for making the photograph is short.

According to recent reports, photographing from a Zodiac adds another dimension to the process. Polar bear presence in East Greenland limits our possibility to operate on land during low-light conditions. Unlike working from stable ground, the shooting position is not necessarily fixed, and even small movements can affect the framing, particularly when using a long focal length.

The objective was to find a viewpoint from which the iceberg formations could be separated visually and the rising moon incorporated without losing the sense of scale. Icebergs are difficult subjects to photograph because their dimensions can be hard to communicate.

Focal length plays an notable role in communicating scale. A wide-angle lens can emphasize the surrounding environment, while a longer lens can compress the scene and bring distant formations visually closer together.

Exposure requires similar care. A gradually brightening moon against a dark sky can make it difficult to preserve highlights without losing detail in the shadows. Rather than trying to make every part of the photograph equally bright, I aim to retain the texture of the illuminated surfaces while allowing darkness to remain part of the image, preserving my highlight and shadow information.

The Northern Lights create a very different set of challenges. The moon’s position can be anticipated, allowing me to plan around a relatively predictable source of illumination. This is great for subject illumination, though distracting when the moon appears in the frame. The aurora, by contrast, can change rapidly in brightness, shape, color, and movement.

In a recent development, from our main vessel, we navigate through the fjord in search of a good-looking iceberg to frame our shot. We carefully position the ship to achieve the greatest possible stability while maintaining the flexibility to adjust our orientation depending on where the aurora is expected to appear. The moment the Northern Lights emerge, close coordination via VHF radio with the bridge team becomes essential. As we prepare to photograph from the ship’s outer deck, the vessel is brought to a complete standstill, reaching zero speed over ground. This allows us to capture the scene with maximum stability, even using exposures of around half a second, while the iceberg and the dancing aurora create the perfect natural composition.

Aurora photography involves a series of compromises between shutter speed, aperture, and ISO. A longer exposure collects more light, which can help when the display is faint, but it can also blur the finer structures of a rapidly moving aurora. A shorter exposure preserves more detail in the curtains and patterns but requires enough light to produce a usable image. There is no universal exposure for the Northern Lights. The right settings depend on the brightness and speed of the display, the available ambient light, the lens, and the amount of detail I want to retain. I adjust according to the behavior of the sky rather than relying on a fixed recipe, as shown below with this powerful curtain of light.

As the sun began to set, we left the comfort of our main vessel and ventured out aboard our Zodiacs for a reconnaissance ride through the surrounding waters. Our mission was to explore the landscape, identify one or two particularly striking icebergs, and select the perfect setting for what we hoped would become an unforgettable night of aurora photography. Capturing the Northern Lights is as much about patience and preparation as it is about being in the right place at the right time. With exposures ranging from half a second to four, five, or even six seconds, stability becomes essential. Even the slightest movement can compromise an image. Out here, surrounded by the vastness of the polar landscape, finding a way to create a stable photographic platform would be one of the greatest challenges of the night.

Sources indicate that our idea was to return after dark, launching the Zodiacs from the main vessel and navigating through the freezing waters in search of newly formed sea ice near one of the selected icebergs. This young ice, approximately one centimeter thick, offered the possibility of carefully positioning the bow of a Zodiac against its edge, allowing us to wedge ourselves into place and create the stability required for long exposures. Finding a sufficiently wide area of newly formed ice would also give us the freedom to reposition ourselves as the auroras shifted and danced across different parts of the sky. But this was about more than simply finding a stable platform. It was about finding the right perspective, in pitch darkness surrounded by the freezing Greenlandic waters.

In a recent development, when planning an operation like this, I always look for ways to approach an iceberg while maintaining a safe distance and shooting from as low an angle as possible. I want the iceberg to become a powerful element in the composition, rising beneath the aurora and giving the image a strong sense of scale and depth. The newly formed sea ice often adds another dimension to the scene. Its delicate patterns, textures, and natural leading lines can guide the viewer’s eye toward the main subject, transforming an already extraordinary landscape into a compelling photographic composition.

By 11 p.m., it was time. We left the main vessel and began our night mission. Alongside my teammates Signe-Maria and Myriam, I led our group of photographers toward the giant icebergs and the newly formed sea ice. Behind us, the ship’s powerful searchlight illuminated our chosen iceberg, providing a guiding beacon across the darkness as we made our way toward our destination. Once we reached the area, we carefully positioned the Zodiacs against the edge of the newly formed ice. Every movement had to be deliberate. We wanted to achieve the stability needed for photography while maintaining a safe distance from the iceberg and the surrounding ice.

Fortunately, we had prepared for this moment long before leaving the ship. During the day, we had already assembled, adjusted, and practiced our photographic setups, making sure everyone knew exactly what to do. Now, under the darkness of the polar night, there was no time to waste. We secured our tripods against the Zodiac’s pontoon and tilted them forward, carefully adjusting their position to keep every part of the Zodiac out of the frame. One by one, our photographers settled into their compositions, pointing their cameras toward the magnificent icebergs.

Everything was ready. I picked up the radio and called the ship’s bridge team, asking them to switch off all the lights. And suddenly, everything changed. The powerful beam that had guided us across the darkness disappeared. We were now completely immersed in the polar night, resting on the newly formed sea ice, facing a gigantic iceberg beneath an extraordinary celestial spectacle. Above us, twenty billion stars seemed to fill the sky. A half-moon gently illuminated the frozen landscape, revealing the magnificent shapes and textures of the iceberg, while the auroras began dancing overhead, bringing movement and color to an otherwise silent world.

For a moment, everything seemed to stand still. There we were, floating between the ocean and the ice, surrounded by one of the most extraordinary landscapes on Earth. Cameras were clicking, shutters were opening and closing, and each long exposure was capturing a fleeting moment of this ever-changing spectacle. It is difficult to describe the feeling of witnessing such a scene. You can blueprint every detail, prepare your equipment, study the conditions, and carefully orchestrate the entire operation, but nature always has the final word. And when everything finally comes together, the experience goes far beyond photography. That night, we were fortunate enough to experience something truly exceptional. A moment in which preparation, teamwork, adventure, and nature converged beneath the dancing auroras. The photographs will remain on our SD cards, but the feeling of being there, surrounded by the icebergs, the stars, and the silence of the polar night, will remain with us forever.

There is a tendency to describe photographs of the Arctic as the result of being in the right place at the right time. Luck certainly plays a role. The moon must rise in a favorable position, the weather must allow the landscape to be seen, and the aurora must develop in a way that creates an interesting composition. None of these conditions can be guaranteed. But being present when a spectacle occurs is only part of the process. The photographer must recognize the potential of the scene, decide where to position the camera, choose a focal length, balance the exposure, and determine which elements belong in the frame. Preparation does not control nature; it makes it possible to respond when an opportunity appears.

“We're not saying they're perfect” indicates architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers.
  • Revealed by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.
  • According to recent reports, officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

It has been revealed that architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Revealed by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

According to recent reports, officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these refurbishment studies need to occur.”.

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.

“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”.

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

In a recent development, robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

Formerly home to approximately 1,500 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s high-rise public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

New facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Industry observers note that energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he mentioned.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the upcoming homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he said.

“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re presently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”.

According to recent reports, the issue is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are right now over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” stated Robinson.

“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”.

Industry observers note that office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Issues Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Vale Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” mentioned Robinson.

“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”.

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.

“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he remarked.

It has been revealed that “The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”.

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the big-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” remarked Robinson.

According to recent reports, “It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental complications. We’re alone.”.

Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

Photography by Ben Hosking, Michael Pham.

Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation.
  • The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected.
  • Sources indicate that “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But newly introduced research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

Sources indicate that “These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

Industry observers note that the research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

It has been revealed that the researchers discovered that while participants said they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”.

In a recent development, ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh indicates. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”.

Sources indicate that people are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher indicates she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”.

It has been revealed that these chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

It has been revealed that “Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen states. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Industry observers note that loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a big impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen notes.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan notes. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan indicates. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”.

It has been revealed that ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she says. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”.

#137309. Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3000 w)

Layered Compositions Will Level Up Your Landscape Photography

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale.
  • Industry observers note that creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another.
  • In a recent development, getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A landscape can look dramatically different in person than it does in a photograph, particularly when a scene loses its sense of depth and scale. Explore how thoughtful layering brings distant views to life by connecting nearby details with the features that make a location memorable.

Industry observers note that creating depth in landscape photography starts with understanding how different parts of a scene relate to one another. Foreground details establish scale, middle-ground features connect the viewer to the wider landscape, and distant elements provide context. When these elements complement one another, they give the photograph greater dimension and draw the viewer through the frame.

In a recent development, getting those elements to work together takes more than placing an interesting subject in the foreground or pointing the camera at a dramatic mountain range. Camera position, focal length, overlapping shapes, and changing light all influence how layers appear and how easily the viewer can distinguish them. This guide explores how to apply these techniques in the field—from recognizing natural layers and arranging them within the frame to avoiding visual clutter.

According to recent reports, the foundation of a layered landscape composition is the relationship between its foreground, middle ground, and background. These three zones provide a visual structure that communicates distance and gives the viewer a sense of moving through the scene. The foreground is the area closest to the camera, the middle ground occupies the space between the viewer and the distant scenery, and the background typically contains the farthest elements, such as mountains, hills, or the sky.

It has been revealed that each layer serves a distinct purpose. The foreground anchors the immediate setting and gives the viewer an entry point. The middle ground bridges that starting point to the rest of the landscape, while the background provides context, scale, and a sense of distance. When these elements work together, the photograph feels far more dimensional than a composition built around a single distant subject.

Recent findings suggest that not every landscape needs three clearly defined layers. A photograph of a mountain reflected in a lake, for example, might rely on two dominant planes, while a forest scene could contain several overlapping layers of trees. The goal is not to force every scene into a rigid formula, but to recognize the distinct planes of distance within it and decide how each contributes to the composition.

In a recent development, before setting up the camera, take a moment to identify what occupies each part of the view. Look for elements that naturally lead the eye through the frame, as well as areas that might compete for attention. Taking this step helps determine whether the scene already has a strong visual structure or whether changing your position could reveal a more effective arrangement.

A strong foreground gives a landscape photograph an immediate point of entry. Rocks, grasses, wildflowers, fallen trees, shoreline details, and other nearby features establish a sense of place while making the distance feel more pronounced. Rather than simply filling the bottom of the frame, the foreground should serve a clear purpose in the composition.

It has been revealed that look for foreground elements that relate to the larger scene. A line of rocks leading toward a mountain, a patch of wildflowers beneath a distant ridgeline, or a weathered tree framing a valley can connect the viewer to the landscape beyond. These details establish scale and make an expansive scene feel more tangible.

Camera position has a considerable effect on how prominent the foreground becomes. Lowering the camera gives nearby objects greater visual weight, often exaggerating their apparent size relative to the background. This can create a dramatic sense of depth, particularly when using a wide-angle lens. However, getting too close can make a foreground object overwhelm the rest of the photograph. Move the camera forward and backward while checking how much space the foreground occupies and whether it remains connected to the distant view.

It has been revealed that pay attention to the edges of the frame as well. A partially cropped rock, branch, or other object along the border can look accidental if it draws attention without adding to the composition. Sometimes shifting the camera just a few inches is enough to position the foreground more deliberately. If there is no suitable foreground element, resist the urge to include something merely to fill the space. A clean, uncomplicated foreground is often more effective than one that distracts from the landscape.

According to recent reports, the middle ground is often the most overlooked part of a landscape composition. Photographers frequently concentrate on finding an interesting foreground and capturing a dramatic background, leaving the space between them without a clear visual role. Yet this middle zone is essential because it bridges near and distant elements, helping the photograph feel cohesive.

Middle-ground subjects can include rolling hills, tree lines, rivers, fields, valleys, waterfalls, or clusters of rocks. These features smooth the transition between planes of distance and can create a natural path through the image. A river winding between a foreground shoreline and distant mountains, for example, gives the viewer a route through the landscape. A series of hills can create successive bands that gradually recede toward the horizon.

Look for shapes and lines that link different parts of the scene. A sloping hillside might echo the angle of a nearby rock formation, while a line of trees could guide attention toward a distant peak. Repeating forms also help unify a composition; a series of ridges or tree-covered slopes creates a visual rhythm that reinforces depth.

Sources indicate that if the middle ground feels empty, consider whether changing your position reveals more of the landscape between the foreground and background. Moving laterally along a trail or shoreline can shift the relationship between overlapping features and expose details that were previously hidden. You may also find that a slightly longer focal length brings distant layers together more effectively, especially in landscapes with repeating hills or ridgelines.

Recent findings suggest that the background gives a landscape its broader context, but distant elements can easily lose definition when they blend together. A mountain peak that merges with a similarly toned ridge, for example, may lose its shape and visual impact. Creating separation between background features preserves their individual forms and reinforces the sense of distance.

According to recent reports, light and weather often provide natural separation. Sidelighting reveals the contours of distant mountains, while low-angle sunlight casts alternating bands of brightness and shadow across hillsides. Fog, mist, and atmospheric haze also distinguish successive layers by reducing contrast as the landscape recedes. These conditions produce subtle tonal transitions that make distant features appear farther away.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

It has been revealed that camera position matters, too. A slight change in elevation or angle can separate a mountain from the ridge behind it or reveal a gap between two overlapping peaks. Before taking the photograph, examine the outlines of distant features and look for places where they merge. Moving even a short distance can create enough separation to make the shapes easier to read.

Exposure also affects how well those details are retained. Bright skies behind dark mountains often create a wide dynamic range, particularly at sunrise and sunset. Check the histogram and highlight warnings to avoid losing notable sky detail. If necessary, use exposure bracketing or a graduated neutral density filter to manage the difference in brightness. Preserving tonal detail across the scene helps maintain the distinction between distant layers.

Recent findings suggest that overlap is one of the most direct ways to communicate depth in a landscape photograph. When one object partially obscures another, the viewer immediately recognizes that the two elements occupy different planes of distance. A foreground tree overlapping a distant ridge, for example, creates a clear spatial relationship even though the photograph is a two-dimensional image.

In a recent development, look for natural arrangements where landscape features overlap cleanly. Successive mountain ridges, layers of trees, and rolling hills are particularly useful because they provide repeated shapes at different distances. The viewer can follow these forms as they recede into the background, creating a sense of depth without requiring a prominent foreground subject.

How much elements overlap also matters. If one element completely hides another, the relationship between them becomes less obvious. If the objects barely touch, their outlines can merge into an awkward visual intersection. Small changes in camera position can reveal more of one feature or create a cleaner separation between them.

According to recent reports, this is especially key when photographing forests or densely layered landscapes. Branches and tree trunks can easily intersect in ways that make the image feel tangled. Rather than trying to include every interesting tree, look for openings where individual trunks and branches remain distinguishable. A slight shift to the left or right may separate one tree from another and make the overall arrangement easier to read.

Focal length directly influences how distance and scale appear in the finished photograph. Wide-angle lenses are useful when the foreground is an notable part of the composition. Their broad field of view captures nearby details alongside distant scenery, while perspective exaggeration between close and far objects emphasizes depth.

Recent findings suggest that when using a wide-angle lens, foreground placement becomes particularly important. An object close to the camera can appear much larger than everything behind it, sometimes dominating the frame. This can be effective when the foreground has a strong shape or texture, but it can also make the composition feel unbalanced. Pay attention to how close you are to the nearest subject and whether its scale supports the relationship between layers.

Industry observers note that telephoto lenses offer a different approach. Rather than emphasizing the distance between foreground and background, longer focal lengths narrow the field of view and make distant features appear closer together. This visual compression can emphasize repeated layers of mountains, hills, trees, or other landscape elements. A scene that looks relatively open through a wide-angle lens may reveal a more graphic arrangement when photographed with a telephoto lens.

Neither approach is inherently better. A wide-angle lens communicates the scale of an expansive landscape, while a telephoto lens isolates a series of distant forms and emphasizes their relationship. If a scene has several interesting layers, try photographing it at different focal lengths before deciding which version best captures the scene.

Light makes layered landscapes more distinctive by revealing shapes, textures, and tonal differences across planes of distance. The same scene may look relatively flat under even midday light but become far more dimensional when low-angle sunlight creates alternating bands of illumination and shadow.

Sidelighting is particularly useful for emphasizing the contours of hills, mountains, and other landforms. As the sun sits low on the horizon, ridges catch the light while valleys remain in shadow. This creates visual separation between successive layers and gives the scene a stronger sense of form. Backlighting can also be effective, especially when photographing trees, grasses, or other translucent elements in the foreground.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Recent findings suggest that atmospheric conditions provide another way to distinguish distance. Mist and fog soften the contrast of distant hills and mountains, creating a series of progressively lighter layers. After a storm, breaks in clearing clouds often spotlight individual sections of a landscape while leaving others in shadow. These changing conditions produce natural divisions between foreground, middle ground, and background without requiring strong compositional elements in every part of the frame.

According to recent reports, when photographing in changing weather, be prepared to work rapidly. Use a tripod when shutter speeds are slow, but avoid relying on one fixed composition if the light is moving across the scene. Take multiple exposures as conditions evolve, particularly when sunlight briefly strikes a distant ridge or a break in the clouds reveals a new layer. These short-lived lighting conditions can make a substantial difference to the finished image.

Adding layers can create depth, but it can also introduce too much visual information. A foreground full of rocks, a middle ground crowded with trees, and a background filled with overlapping mountain peaks may leave the viewer unsure where to look. The challenge is deciding which elements contribute to the photograph and which ones make it harder to read.

Start by identifying the primary subject or visual feature. This does not have to be a single object — it might be a mountain range, a winding river, or a series of repeating ridgelines. Once you know what should attract attention, consider whether the other layers support it. A foreground element that pulls the eye away from the main subject may need to be repositioned or excluded from the frame.

Industry observers note that simplifying a composition does not always mean removing entire layers—it often means adjusting how much visual weight each one carries. A smaller foreground can establish context without competing with the background, while an open middle ground gives the viewer’s eye room to travel through the scene. Switching to a longer focal length can also help trim distracting edges or unrelated elements.

According to recent reports, watch for bright highlights, stray branches, and high-contrast objects that pull attention away from the subject. These distractions become more disruptive in a layered composition, where the viewer’s eye is already navigating multiple planes. Scan the entire frame before pressing the shutter—paying close attention to the corners and edges—for anything that interrupts the visual flow. Often, shifting the camera slightly or tightening the crop is enough to clean up the frame.

Even a minor shift in camera position can alter the relationship between every layer in a landscape. Moving forward or backward changes the scale and placement of foreground objects, while stepping laterally can reveal or conceal distant features. Camera height also dictates how much of the ground plane is visible and how smoothly the foreground transitions into the background.

Rather than immediately setting up a tripod at the first scenic overlook, take time to explore the area. Walk along a ridge, follow a shoreline, or look for a slightly elevated vantage point that opens up the landscape. Observe how foreground elements align with distant peaks, trees, or ridges. Often, the strongest composition sits just a few steps away from the obvious viewpoint.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra).

Industry observers note that once you find a promising spot, a tripod helps you fine-tune height and framing deliberately. Lowering the tripod emphasizes nearby textures, while raising it reveals more of the middle ground. If your tripod has an adjustable center column, extend it sparingly as raising the column too high reduces stability, especially in windy conditions.

It has been revealed that perspective control is also worth considering in scenes with strong vertical lines. Tilting the camera upward causes trees, cliffs, or buildings to converge toward the top of the frame. While that converging effect can work creatively, keeping vertical lines straight requires leveling the camera and adjusting your composition by stepping back or switching to a wider lens. What matters most is whether the perspective reinforces how you want the layers to relate.

Building a layered landscape composition becomes much easier when you approach a scene methodically. Start by identifying the anchor of the view—whether that is a distant peak, a line of trees, a winding river, or light sweeping across a valley. From there, work backward toward the camera to see which nearby elements can serve as an entry point without overpowering the main subject.

In a recent development, once you have identified potential layers, move around to test different arrangements. Look for foreground features that lead naturally into the middle ground, and check how distant shapes overlap. Watch the gaps between objects so unrelated elements do not merge into awkward outlines. If the scene feels overly busy, simplify with a tighter framing or a longer focal length rather than trying to include everything.

According to recent reports, your camera settings should support both the field conditions and the intended depth of the photograph. For a static landscape requiring front-to-back sharpness, a mid-range aperture such as f/8 or f/11 is a reliable starting point. Focus roughly one-third of the way into the scene, then zoom in on your review screen to verify that both the nearest and farthest key elements are sharp. Optimal focus distance depends on focal length, aperture, and proximity to the foreground; if a very close foreground and distant background cannot both be rendered sharply in a single frame, focus stacking is a reliable alternative when the scene is still.

Keep your ISO low when practical, but do not let the pursuit of a noise-free file force an overly slow shutter speed. Wind moving through grasses or foliage often calls for a faster exposure, even if that requires raising your ISO. A tripod eliminates camera shake, but it cannot freeze motion within the landscape itself.

According to recent reports, before leaving a location, photograph the scene using several different focal lengths and compositions. Start with a wider frame that emphasizes the foreground, then try a tighter composition that compresses repeating layers or gives greater weight to the background. I also like revisiting locations under different light and weather, as shifts in atmosphere or time of day can completely transform a scene’s character and yield a more dramatic photograph. Comparing these variations helps reveal which arrangement and conditions best capture the landscape.

Ultimately, layered landscape photography is about building intentional relationships between elements in a scene. Foreground, middle ground, and background offer a reliable structural framework, but their impact depends on how well they connect, overlap, and remain visually distinct. By paying close attention to camera position, focal length, light, and visual balance, you can create landscapes with genuine depth and clarity.

Industry News: Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

It has been revealed that this eventually led to the fresh, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

In a recent development, the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

Sources indicate that the unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a new model of partnership”.

Industry observers note that this week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

According to recent reports, the items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

The earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

In a recent development, the other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

It has been revealed that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

Sources indicate that the five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a new display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Kodak SlideTag Is a $35 Blind-Box E Ink Photo Display and AirTag Alternative

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (463 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, reto, the company behind the wildly successful Kodak Charmera, has declared its next blind box-style product: the Kodak SlideTag.
  • The SlideTag uses that E Ink display to allow owners to upload their own photos into it and display them like single slides from the golden age of film.
  • “When Kodak introduced Kodachrome in 1935, the slide mount swiftly became the classic way people projected and shared their favorite memories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, reto, the company behind the wildly successful Kodak Charmera, has declared its next blind box-style product: the Kodak SlideTag. It’s a small, color E Ink display with AirTag-like capability and a user-replaceable battery.

The SlideTag uses that E Ink display to allow owners to upload their own photos into it and display them like single slides from the golden age of film.

“When Kodak introduced Kodachrome in 1935, the slide mount swiftly became the classic way people projected and shared their favorite memories. Families gathered around glowing projectors, watching their favorite moments illuminated inside a simple cardboard frame,” Reto claims.

“Decades later, the Kodak SlideTag breathes fresh life into that iconic retro slide frame, bringing a vintage touch to the digital age. Designed as a miniature memory holder, it allows you to digitize your precious moments and easily carry your stories wherever you go.”.

The SlideTag measures 39.3(W) x 46(H) x 7.58(D) mm and weighs just 16.6 grams. The central display is 1.54 inches across with a resolution of 240 x 240 pixels. The color E Ink can display up to six colors and because E Ink doesn’t require any power to retain the image, the SlideTag can display a photo and retain other functionality for extended lengths of time without dying.

Recent findings suggest that the “other functionality” that does require battery power is the compatibility with Apple Find My and Google Android Find Hub. The IP54 rated keychain supports Bluetooth 5.4 and has a real-time tracking range of up to 30 meters while also being compatible with both Google and Apple’s tracking networks. The SlideTag can also buzz on command at 75 dB to help locate it.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to supporting photos, the SlideTay also comes with a host of other features such as a custom QR code for displaying social links or digital business cards. It can also display live daily to-do lists, calendars, event countdowns, or personalized name badges. Photos can be set as simple galleries that only change when the button on the back is double pressed or as slideshows that change as often as once per day. All of the features of the SlideTag require connecting to the Kodak Memory Link app.

Reto is offering the Kodak SlideTag in eight standard styles, with one extra secret design style that is substantially rarer than the others: a silver color.

All SlideTags come with a collectible 35mm slide frame that actually fits a real 35mm slide as well as other small collectibles.

The Kodak SlideTag is available starting today for $35 or as a box of eight for $280.
