Kodak SlideTag Review: This E-Ink Equipped, AirTag Keychain Rocks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have near rock-bottom expectations of Reto when it comes to making a good product.
  • The Kodak SlideTag is not only a cute, fun idea, but also legitimately useful and a brilliant way to allow photographers to enjoy their work and keep track of their belongings at the same time.
  • With the exception of the Snapic A1, Reto tends to make very cheap, eye-catching products that don’t stand the test of time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have near rock-bottom expectations of Reto when it comes to making a good product. In my opinion, it’s a better marketing organization than a product manufacturer, and everything it makes is meant to sell swiftly and be forgotten, with the Charmera being the most obvious example. But SlideTag is, somehow, not that. Instead, it is an incredibly good product.

The Kodak SlideTag is not only a cute, fun idea, but also legitimately useful and a brilliant way to allow photographers to enjoy their work and keep track of their belongings at the same time.

With the exception of the Snapic A1, Reto tends to make very cheap, eye-catching products that don’t stand the test of time. My Charmera, for example, is already broken despite not being subjected to anything extreme. Chris Niccolls points to the Charmera as the culprit behind the wave of e-waste we’ve seen from copycats the world over. When we heard that Reto had another blind box-style keychain product coming, our immediate reaction was to sigh in dismay.

But to our true shock, the Reto SlideTag is not only really fun and well-priced, but it’s also legitimately an excellent product.

So what exactly is the Kodak SlideTag? A nostalgic toy? A calendar? A to-do list? A gallery? A slideshow? An AirTag? A keychain?

The answer is yes, and even a little bit more.

At first glance, it’s easy to think that this is going to be yet another piece of junk, but as you dig deeper, you start to realize this is actually not only a useful tool, but also a fun one.

It has been revealed that so yes, it is a keychain styled after classic Kodak slide film holders. The frames come in a total of nine possible styles (eight standard and one “secret” special one), and these are hidden inside of the socially acceptable gambling mechanic: blind boxes.

Industry observers note that reto is very, very good at marketing, and that much is apparent in the whole blind box unboxing experience. The SlideTag is not the only thing in the box: you also get a really nice pamphlet showing all the possible options, a little cardboard slide holder that actually does fit a 35mm slide in it (and Reto includes a Kodak-branded one as an example), and a few other little bits and bobs that just ooze style.

According to recent reports, opening the box is just as much part of the experience as actually seeing which one of the SlideTags you got. Almost all of the SlideTag designs are great, with the exception of the pink one, which I unfortunately pulled from my first box. I call it “pig skin pink” mostly because the sample photo Reto indicates on the “collect them all” chart does, in fact, show a pig on the screen for the pink one. Chris pulled the Kodachrome.

Sources indicate that I acquired two more and also got Kodachrome (which I like a lot) as well as the two-tone green-and-white one. Much better.

The tags themselves have a color E Ink screen that can display photos that you upload to it (up to 12 at a time) and can either be programmed to swap images at a given interval or only change them when you want to by double-clicking the button on the back of the SlideTag. Once an image is uploaded and displayed, it doesn’t take any power to keep the image there, so it should (in theory) last for months.

Even when the battery dies, Reto didn’t go the same route it has with its other blind box toys and actually gives you the ability to swap in a new battery. The SlideTag uses a lithium CR2025 battery, which can be replaced easily by unscrewing a panel on the back of the keychain.

Just having a little rotating gallery of your photos attached to your bag was already a good idea, but Reto went further and made the SlideTag compatible with Apple Find My and Android Find Hub. It is, for all intents and purposes, also an AirTag. Brilliant.

But it does even more than that.

According to recent reports, just being a gallery and an AirTag keychain would have been plenty of value, but Reto kept stacking on the capabilities. In order to use any of these features, though, you do need to download the Kodak Memory Link app. Once open, it is super easy to connect SlideTags to it, and the process is quick and smooth.

The interface will show you a variety of options, including the aforementioned gallery and Find My features, but there is a lot more. You can have it display a to-do list, a calendar, and a countdown (like if you need a reminder of a special event like a birthday). If you’re a content creator, you can also have it display a QR code that it will generate based on a link you give it. This is particularly useful if you’re at a gathering or event where people will be asking for your website, portfolio, or Instagram handle. With this, you can just hold out your SlideTag, and they can go right to it. You can even have it act as a name tag, showing your information if you want to attach this to luggage or wear it as simple identification — the choice is yours.

Recent findings suggest that the charming thing is that as much as there are so many other affordable Find My location devices and keychains that you can buy out on the market, this one’s photographically themed, and I just think that’s smart marketing. Because it has so many more capabilities, it’s a bit more expensive than the alternatives. That mentioned, it’s actually a tag you’ll want to show off and not just stuff in a pocket and never look at.

I think if I were going to have a little Find My location device around the house, why wouldn’t I want it to be Kodak-themed and have things like a gallery and slideshows and the other useful things like the QR code?

Recent findings suggest that reto is a very smart, well-run firm. It knows what to make and what will be a hit, but up until now, the most popular products have also been ones that don’t stand the test of time — they lose their luster in as little as a few minutes, honestly. The Charmera is a perfect example of this, and while I enjoyed it for a few minutes, now mine is just a piece of plastic garbage.

The SlideTag is different. The removable and replaceable battery is a lovely change from a built-in battery that will no doubt eventually die, the utility of the Find My compatibility is amazing, and the combination of that actual, real-world useful feature with a color E Ink display to show off your photos is truly fantastic.

The SlideTag is sold in blind boxes and priced at $35 each. You can also buy a set of eight for $280. That’s more expensive than other tracking tag options, but it also does more. It’s up to you if what Reto offers here is worth that $5 to $10 premium. I, for one, think it definitely is.

In a recent development, there is really nothing quite like this… yet. I’m sure that, just like the Charmera, Reto will be promptly knocked off on AliExpress, but for now, it’s truly unique. You can get an E Ink display, and you can get tracking tags, but you can’t get something that’s both.

Apple AirTagBuy newly introduced on B&HApple AirTagBuy used on KEH.comGoogle Pixel TagBuy new on B&HGoogle Pixel TagBuy used on KEH.com.

If you’re just interested in the tracking feature, the Apple AirTag, Google Pixel Tag, and Xiaomi Tag are all just as capable (or more so, given the network they use to provide specific locations) and are cheaper. They just don’t look nearly as cool dangling off your bag or keys.

Sources indicate that yes. The Kodak SlideTag is not only a cute, fun idea, but also legitimately useful and a brilliant way to allow photographers to enjoy their work and keep track of their belongings at the same time.

Industry News: Carolina Zimbalist pours bioplastic over silk for Emma Watson's LACMA Gala dress

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rich Stapleton.

Artist Carolina Zimbalist has co-created a biomaterial dress with actress Emma Watson, who wore it at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s 15th annual Art+Film Gala.

Zimbalist, a graduate of the Parsons School of Design, employed a homemade bioplastic she frequently uses in her artistic works in order to create the one-of-a-kind garment, which comprises a longline bodice and floor-length skirt rendered in shades of red.

The petroleum-free poured-and-dried material, containing vegetable glycerin alongside naturally derived proteins such as pea powder, is layered over silk – a natural biopolymer itself.

“The formulation draws on naturally derived proteins and other ingredients, with the exact composition varying depending on what I’m making,” Zimbalist told Dezeen.

“Very often I favour the usage of byproducts.”.

The material’s technical makeup lends itself to a distinctive aesthetic once poured and dried.

“My biomaterial creates sculptural forms and flexible surfaces that move with the body,” said Zimbalist.

“The visual qualities are meant to draw greater interest in sustainable materials while remaining fundamentally artistic.”.

Zimbalist has variously referred to her recipe as a bioplastic, a biomaterial or a biopolymer, but now favours the latter to avoid negative associations with the term “plastic”.

“For years, I described my formulas as bioplastics, but about three seasons ago, I switched to ‘biomaterials’; when people hear ‘bioplastic’, they tend to focus on the plastic,” Zimbalist continued.

Industry observers note that “‘Biomaterial’ opens up a different conversation about what the material is and what it can become. All three terms apply, but they bring different associations – although biopolymer is the most technically accurate.”.

Zimbalist hopes that by experimenting with these natural materials, they can become a mainstream and accessible means of constructing garments beyond one-off pieces.

“The environmental benefits are something I’m developing along with the growing wave of biomaterial artists now assembling – I like to think we are presenting sustainable fashion in a way that inspires more interest beyond the fringes.”.

Zimbalist is no stranger to clothing celebrities: 2024 saw musician Chapelle Roan wear a hand-painted, garden-inspired dress that the artist made partially using seaweed.

As well as garments, the artist also creates ethereal and sculptural homeware, including lighting and vases.

Biomaterials are sweeping the fashion world, opening up opportunities for aesthetic and sustainable progress in a sector not historically known for its eco-friendliness.

Designers are increasingly finding ways to derive materials, fabrics and ornamentation from pioneering sources, including mycelium, tree cellulose and soil.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The first thing you see is the space between the letters.
  • Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

The first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

The type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

Sources indicate that the old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The new system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

Recent findings suggest that colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

The system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Industry observers note that feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

According to recent reports, before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

Industry observers note that how you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a latest opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date].".

Industry observers note that the transition blueprint: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

Industry observers note that side hustlers! With the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card you can earn free travel from your business expenses.

Sources indicate that chooseFI has partnered with CardRatings for our coverage of credit card products. ChooseFI and CardRatings may receive a commission from card issuers.

Conventional advice claims never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

It has been revealed that if you are leaving due to tech giant changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:.

According to recent reports, COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

Sources indicate that ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

In a recent development, here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Recent findings suggest that the FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

In a recent development, have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the matter your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

In a recent development, verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Sources indicate that before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the problem 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

Recent findings suggest that COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

It has been revealed that the question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees.
  • According to recent reports, the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in.
  • Recent findings suggest that before the auction, Sotheby’s had not revealed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.

According to recent reports, the auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the Upcoming York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (May 1890).

Recent findings suggest that before the auction, Sotheby’s had not revealed a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.

Industry observers note that the uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).

Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).

The previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.

In a recent development, sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”.

Literaturport.de via Wikimedia Commons.

News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the Fresh York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?

In response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.

In a recent development, urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.

Industry observers note that comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the Fresh York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.

It has been revealed that then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.

Following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a new owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”.

The terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.

Title page of the Leicester Galleries exhibition Artists who Died Young, with an image of Blossoming Chestnut Trees.

Recent findings suggest that as a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to New York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin Bailey’s recent Van Gogh books.

In a recent development, martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

According to recent reports, his other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com.

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

Yuri Suzuki 3D-prints miniature rollercoaster and Ferris wheel for kinetic Onomatopia exhibition

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Designer Yuri Suzuki drew on his childhood fascination with amusement parks for the Onomatopia exhibition, which features playful dioramas with their own soundtracks and shows how theme parks “bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience”.
  • On show at the Osh Gallery in London’s Angel neighbourhood, the exhibition features five models, a short film and reference materials from Suzuki’s own archive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Chris Kidall Park (unless otherwise stated).

Designer Yuri Suzuki drew on his childhood fascination with amusement parks for the Onomatopia exhibition, which features playful dioramas with their own soundtracks and shows how theme parks “bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience”.

On show at the Osh Gallery in London’s Angel neighbourhood, the exhibition features five models, a short film and reference materials from Suzuki’s own archive.

The dioramas – a Ferris wheel, rollercoaster, helter-skelter, dodgems and carousel – resemble some of Suzuki‘s earlier work, such as the interactive Sonic Bloom installation in London.

“The ideas have existed in my sketchbooks for the last couple of years and have gradually developed through a series of my public art projects,” Suzuki told Dezeen.

“I’ve always been interested in expanding the scale of my sound sculptures, imagining how they might eventually become architectural structures or even full-scale amusement park rides.”.

The designer 3D-printed the kinetic sculptures, which move and are accompanied by their own soundtracks, from polylactic acid (PLA) plastic.

“The dioramas are mainly made using 3D-printed materials, alongside modified HO-scale miniature structures,” he said.

“I had picked up traditional amusement park components – roller coaster, ferris wheel, helter-skelter, carousel, and dodge cars – to visualise my ideas for sound sculptures and architectural structures that could potentially be realised on a larger scale in the future.”.

Suzuki has been drawn to amusement parks all his life, and with Onomatopia he wanted to explore how they could help create a utopian city.

“I’ve been fascinated by theme parks since I was a child, particularly Disneyland, but also the relationship between amusement parks, world expos and urban planning, from Coney Island as explored in Rem Koolhaas’s Delirious Newly introduced York to the 1889 Paris Exposition,” he explained.

“I had the opportunity to work with Disney Imagineering, who create Disney parks, and I became particularly interested in Walt Disney’s original vision for EPCOT (Experimental Prototype of Community of Tomorrow),” Suzuki continued.

“It imagined an ideal city rather than simply a theme park, and Onomatopia is my own attempt to imagine a utopian city shaped by sound, drawing on my experience creating public installations.”.

Suzuki, who is known for his sound design, has previously created pieces such as an acoustic playground in Shanghai and a “trumpet-like” San Francisco art installation.

“For me, theme parks and expos are fascinating because they bring together architecture, sound, movement and human experience within an imagined world, almost like an experiment in creating a utopian city,” Suzuki explained.

The designer drew on his experience of working on a large-scale sound design when creating these smaller versions of his sculptures.

“Over the last couple of years I have been involved in some large city development projects, such as creating Metropolis Symphony for One Bangkok and my initial involvement in planning around the V&A East (East Bank) development,” Suzuki said.

“I’ve become increasingly interested in how sound can shape public spaces, and my own idea of utopia is a place where sound contributes to wellbeing and encourages communication between people, beyond the boundaries of language and culture.”.

Recent findings suggest that onomatopia is on show at Osh Gallery, The Old Sorting House, 46 Essex Road, London from 10 November 2026 to 7 January 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Photography by Chris Kidall Park (unless otherwise stated).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).

Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.

Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.

According to recent reports, raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.

Detail of Carolina Caycedo, "Neodymium Intensive" (2026), colored pencil, aluminum and variegated metal leaf on paper (left); Installation view of "Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Major Dipper and North Star" (2023) at Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots at the Kemper Art Museum.

Industry observers note that like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Major Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.

Sources indicate that across the Mississippi River, as part of the Counterpublic 2026 triennial, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.

At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.

Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4. The installation, "Fiesta de la Raíces," part of Counterpublic 2026, will be on view at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition at the Kemper was curated by Meredith Malone and "Fiesta de la Raíces" was curated by James McAnally.

#137297. Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (888 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity.
  • Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.
  • At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

It has been revealed that “Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

They also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik states.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik indicates. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”.

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

Sources indicate that “Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik indicates. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

It has been revealed that the steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”.

Still, it’s vital to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

One of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she states.

In fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik says.

It has been revealed that both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

Industry observers note that if you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik claims. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

But if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik says.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s vital to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

Recent findings suggest that “Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik says. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”.

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Industry observers note that ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative.
  • Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SomeOne broke the Co-op symbol into five Membershapes for the latest Co-op brand identity, putting member ownership at the heart of the system.

According to recent reports, co-op has been owned by its members since 1844, when thirteen Rochdale Pioneers founded the world's first consumer cooperative. Nearly 2,400 stores and more than five million members later, that fact still sets it apart, and SomeOne built the whole Brandworld on it. Under creative director Shaun Turnbull, the studio took the cloverleaf Co-op had brought back eight years before and broke it into five pieces, the Membershapes. Each piece is one of the mark's most recognisable forms, strong enough to stand alone, and together they carry the idea that every member owns a piece of Co-op. The shapes work as windows, holding devices, patterns and graphic devices, so the same blue field can hold a billboard headline, a phone screen price or a tote bag pattern, and the system still reads as one brand across Food, Funeralcare, Insurance and Legal Services.

The type does the shouting. Co-op Headline is the co-operative's first bespoke typeface, drawn with F37 from the DNA of the symbol. The squircle-like corners and angled cuts on the c and p come straight from the mark, and the face is built to run in caps, loud and straight. SomeOne also made a textured version, an SVG cut with an ink-rolled texture created at St Bride Library in London, so the letters keep the uneven bite of letterpress blocks. The specimen sheet highlights the alphabet at full size, texture visible in every stroke, with the numbers set underneath in the same weight. On posters and app screens the type sits inside a Membershape, the shape doing the layout work while the caps do the talking.

The texture is the finish. That ink-rolled grain runs through the type, the shapes and the membership card, giving a national supermarket the feel of a printed pamphlet. History gets the same treatment: the old dividend stamps, the divi, return as a full sheet of blue stamps, each carrying the mark and a number, a direct line from 1844 to the present. Around it, the system stays practical. A lorry carries 'We're member driven' across a blue side panel, the app screens stack member prices and store finding under the same shapes, and the tote bag wears the Membershape pattern outright. An expressive icon set, drawn from the curves of the symbol, extends the language to every touchpoint, and the ambition is plain: grow membership from five million to eight million by 2030.

Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.

The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

Industry News: Finding, acquiring and showing off: how rich buyers use social media to build art collections

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world?
  • In a recent development, while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media.
  • The data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that how do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, shows that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.

In a recent development, while the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report claims.

The data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report claims. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”.

In a recent development, when it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents said they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).

A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.

Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also highlighted that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.

According to recent reports, the importance of ​​online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among latest collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.

But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.

Sources indicate that the report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data highlighted that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".

In a recent development, “Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”.

When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Made Thought builds the Juana brand identity on acid lime and amber, a CBD skincare system where dense label type meets macro botanical light.

Juana is a CBD-powered skincare brand, and Made Thought frames it as half family tradition, half skincare innovation. Founder Yann Moujawaz comes from a line of surgeons and Syrian olive grove stewards, and his formulations aim to switch on the skin's own renewal with expert precision. The design answers a market full of noise and false claims with something that looks like proof: warm amber glass, clinical label density, and botanical photography shot like evidence. The palette does the arguing. Acid lime cuts against deep olive and burnt orange, and the amber packs glow against it all like samples held up to the light.

The wordmark is a compact grotesque JUANA in capitals, set small and quiet on every pack, letting the label copy do the talking. On the lime tubes, ingredient lists run down the barrel in tight bilingual columns, English beside French, with the CBD strength called out large: 100mg on the cleanser, 300mg on the face cream, plus vitamin E, jojoba oil, and hyaluronic acid in the same breath.

According to recent reports, at poster scale the same type goes loud. Nurture Facial Cleanser, 100mg CBD fills the frame in acid lime, underlined, with the pack leaning into the shot. The web panel pairs a flat lime block reading Full Spectrum Cannabinoids with a hand dipping into a jar, and a line-drawn diagram of the whole range sits on olive like a spec sheet. The system holds together because the grid never changes, only the scale does.

The materials carry the science half of the story. Amber glass keeps the formulas away from the light, frosted lime plastic softens the tubes, and matte black caps close every silhouette. White outer cartons stack in a stepped row with a single lime band along the top edge, the only colour the box allows itself. Macro shots push closer still: a pipette suspended in fortifying face oil, bubbles rising through amber, and a leaf photographed so tight its veins turn into a map of yellow, green, and blue.

Founder Yann Moujawaz calls the partnership magic, saying passion was generously poured into it, and the photography backs him up. Nothing here is styled to look expensive for its own sake. The glow comes from the product itself, amber oil against orange light, and the identity lets it show.

American fast-food chain Chipotle has launched a hoodie with a hidden, insulated pocket built for one highly specific purpose.

The novelty streetwear garment was designed to keep burritos both warm and concealed while sneaking them into the cinema for illicit mid-movie snacking.

Accessed via a subtle zip at the top of the hoodie’s front pouch, the pocket can also squeeze in an entire burrito bowl or a set of tacos, Chipotle claims, although the logistics of that might be trickier.

Kirby Ann Connell, the manufacturer’s senior director of social and influencers, mentioned the launch was inspired by real stories of people smuggling elaborate Chipotle meals into the cinema.

Recent findings suggest that “Movie nights deserve real, craveable food,” she said. “And since our fans were already sneaking Chipotle to theatres, we figured we’d make it a little easier.”.

“Sometimes innovation is as simple as putting a burrito pocket in a hoodie,” she added.

The limited-edition Sneak It In hoodie features an oversized fit to conceal any bulky contraband, plus a dedicated napkin pocket for any spills.

It comes in three colourways: Nothing To See Here Black, No Burrito Here Brown and Got the Goods Gray.

Chipotle is the latest brand to create novelty streetwear as a marketing stunt.

Other offerings include KFC’s Pickle Puffer, Lego-shaped Crocs and Aldi’s Potato Jacket.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation.
  • Landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, the site of US president Donald Trump‘s proposed triumphal arch.
  • Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city’s historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation.

Landscape architecture students at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design have designed two proposals for Memorial Circle in Washington, DC, the site of US president Donald Trump‘s proposed triumphal arch.

Both designs feature expansive pools of water that cover the current vehicular roundabout at Memorial Circle, and emphasise connectivity to the city’s historic processional axis and straight sightlines to the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery.

It has been revealed that the students, Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, worked with Washington DC non profit organisation The Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF) on the designs. The aim was to engage the public in the design process, as the team views the government did not properly open the arch up for review.

“By recognising Memorial Circle’s implicit expressions of monumentality, this pair of counter proposals asserts design’s capacity to critically engage history, accommodate public life, and advocate on behalf of our shared cultural landscape,” said Dvorak and Geitner.

The project began after Dvork and Geitner attended a seminar at the GSD taught by TCLF founding partner Charles A Birnbaum.

“As graduate students in landscape architecture, we took Birnbaum’s course to ground our emerging practices in critical historical inquiry and public participation,” they said.

“The current administration’s assertion of authority over national memory presented an opportunity to put these convictions into practice.”.

The first proposal treats Memorial Circle as “a void along the historic axis between Washington and Arlington”. The designers chose to fill the central roundabout circle, at the moment covered by grass, with a low-lying pool of water.

A natural stone perimeter surrounds the pool and is inscribed with words of “belonging and unity”.

It’s design is “restrained” according to the team, and primarily meant to be viewed from a vehicle while passing through the traffic circle.

The second proposal does away with the traffic circle entirely and instead inserts a straight thoroughfare to Arlington Memorial Bridge.

Two circular fountains would be located on either side of the road. Additionally, a large pool of water, mirroring the perimeter of the former traffic circle, would fill up the site during commemorative events when the bridge is closed.

It draws upon previous historical proposals for Memorial Circle and seeks to pay homage to the precedent of the site.

“[The fountain] geometries arise from the site’s historic proposals, combining concentric circles, intersecting alignments, and formal planting into a composition that acknowledges history whilst creating its own present identity,” said the designers.

“In this way the landscape becomes a physical record of its own change.”.

Industry observers note that trump’s proposed arch was unveiled late last year with renderings by US studio Harrison Design. It features gilded statues and a neoclassical design and has been dubbed the “Arc de Trump” – a play on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

Construction on the arch was set to begin in September with the government barreling ahead, but it was halted in early November by Judge Tanya S Chutkan.

Trump has claimed the arch will serve as a “military complex” with snipers in an attempt to use national security as a pretext for construction.

Many take problem with the arch blocking views to adjacent Arlington Cemetery, including members of the Kennedy family, who filed a lawsuit to block construction, claiming that the arch would cast shadows over the grave of president John F Kennedy.

The US Commission of Fine Arts (CFA), which reviews projects in the capital city, approved the project in May.

The proposals also follow recent efforts by the legislature to change Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider the impact of proposed projects on historic properties.

Recent findings suggest that earlier in November, protesters gathered in Washington DC in opposition of the administration’s proposed rewrite of these protections. They are couched within the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) bill recently introduced to Congress.

Images by Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn’t find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

“How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen. “So I’m never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it’s just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece.”.

It has been revealed that “I’ve never been so inspired by design in general,” she added. “It’s a skill that fits very well to me, but I’d rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline.”.

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she indicates she wouldn’t have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

“I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them,” she explained. “For me, it’s sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be.”.

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year’s Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

Explaining the studio’s decision to select her as a 20×20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder’s approach for being “both remarkably gentle and quietly bold”.

“Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked,” the studio told Dezeen.

Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).

These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder’s studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.

“I’m inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings,” she said. “I think it’s just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design.”.

“In the history of architecture there’s so much to tell,” she continued. “For me it’s more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that’s what interests me so much.”.

Recent findings suggest that “And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration.”.

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.

In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder’s atelier space.

She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

In a recent development, in the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing. Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.

In a recent development, “I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well,” said Tangelder. “The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn’t really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more new for me.”.

Sources indicate that “I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years,” she considered. “There’s a lot happening right now.”.

It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.

Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.

Sources indicate that “That has been super vital for me,” she said. “Each material that I really love, I have a partner now.”.

Industry observers note that but moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.

“I really like it, so for me it’s the best way to spend my time,” she noted, before pausing.

“I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it’s also a struggle. You’re always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made.”.

Recent findings suggest that so that means you take risks all the time. It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.

Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

“In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing,” she remembered. “Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.”.

Over time, she notes she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.

“I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental,” she explained.

“So that means you take risks all the time,” she added. “It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.”.

Most of Tangelder’s work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.

A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.

This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.

Recent findings suggest that I just think the material is very me. That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.

It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.

Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.

“So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process,” she stated.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Tangelder’s current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.

“I just think the material is very me,” she remarked. “That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.”.

Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.

And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.

In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.

She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.

For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.

“I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it’s also a reaction to what he’s done,” she said.

“He’s so clear in the decisions that he makes, he’s a master in it, and I’m really grateful that he sees what I’ve been doing.”.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College revealed Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in Fresh York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”.
