📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s a common assumption that great, adventurous sex is a young person’s game—and with age, it fades into something boring, nonexistent, or just…not worth the effort.

Recent findings suggest that growing up, Karen Bigman fell for the propaganda. “But recently, I’ve done it in restaurant bathrooms,” Bigman, a 62-year-old certified sex educator, tells SELF, before listing off other examples of her scandalous escapades. “I’ve spontaneously met up in hotel rooms when the kids were at home. We even pulled over next to a Duane Reade [convenience store], under the fluorescent lamp, to do it in the back seat of his car.”.

To be clear, sex isn’t always this spontaneous for Bigman. But in both her own life and her work with clients, she insists sex in this stage of life isn’t just happening: It’s getting better. For some, it’s even kinkier—though it’s a reality you rarely hear about and probably don’t want to imagine your parents or grandparents doing.

The fear that your sex life dies with age doesn’t come from nowhere. Bodies change. Menopause (which typically starts in a person’s 40s or 50s) can bring on a slew of symptoms like vaginal dryness or painful sex. Hormonal shifts can lower libido across all sexes. Energy levels fluctuate—and acting out on desires that once felt automatic may now require more effort, communication, and patience.

Still, none of this has to spell the end of a satisfying bedroom life, according to both sex therapists and real people enjoying sex after 60. Here’s how they maintain the spark—and the small shifts they say make the biggest differences.

Vaginal dryness is one of the most common physical changes that comes with aging—and it’s why many people assume getting frisky in this stage will be uncomfortable or painful.

Recent findings suggest that however, there are plenty of expert-recommended products designed to help, and lube is one of the most effective and underrated. “Put it on before you start and have it at the ready during sex,” Bigman, who also shares her advice on her Taboo to Truth: Life & Sex After 50 podcast, says. Lubricants work by reducing friction, which means less risk of irritation or tearing—and just as importantly, more room for pleasure. For best results, we also recommend applying it not just to the penetrating object (like a penis or vibrator) and what’s being penetrated (your vagina), but also during foreplay—for example, consider sliding between labial folds too. (If you’re unsure what lube to buy, start with this beginner-friendly article.).

Recent findings suggest that in some situations, the issue may not be physical or logistical. It’s that the sex you’re having just…isn’t that great.

Industry observers note that “If you’re in a relationship or marriage where sex is not exciting, of course you’re not going to want to do it,” Tammy Nelson, PhD, a 63-year-old AASECT-certified sex therapist, who also speaks from personal experience, tells SELF. “It’s like, if the party isn’t fun, why would you go?”.

However, one of the many upsides of getting older is acquiring a kind of bluntness your younger self probably shied away from. “At a certain point, you just don’t give a crap,” one 64-year-old woman, speaking anonymously, tells SELF. When you realize life’s too short, you stop worrying so much about how your body looks in certain lighting, how you sound while climaxing, and whether your kinks are “too much.”.

“I was once so ashamed to bring up BDSM—being spanked, choked. You don’t want to scare someone off or be judged,” she notes. But after years of what she calls “vanilla sex,” she discovered a game-changing truth: speaking up is worth it. “I had my first real orgasm—that I didn’t have to fake—at 61.”.

Achieving a mind-blowing climax doesn’t require a partner. For the women SELF spoke with, their 50s and 60s marked a turning point in figuring out what made them squirm—where they enjoyed being touched, what kind of stimulation worked, which fantasies excited them—all thanks to masturbation.

According to recent reports, “I feel freer now to explore my body,” Shay Martin, 63, who owns Vibratex (the exclusive distributor of the Magic Wand sex toy brand), tells SELF. “When I was younger, I would use my hands manually, but there are so many tools out there [vibrators, anal toys, penis rings, nipple clamps] to help with achieving an orgasm on your own that’s much more intense and lasts longer.”.

Research backs up the benefits of solo play: Not only does masturbation feel great, but it can also boost confidence in your sexuality (something older women are rarely encouraged to embrace) and relieve menopause-related symptoms like vaginal dryness, low sex drive, and mood changes. Once you figure out what feels good, “it becomes a whole lot easier to communicate exactly what you want from another person,” Dr. Nelson says—which makes settling for mediocre hookups (the kind you may have tolerated in your 20s) far less likely.

Bodies in their 60s don’t always cooperate the way they used to—and that’s okay.

Industry observers note that an aching back and weak knees have made certain positions uncomfortable for Isma, 68. “Standard missionary can be tough, so I usually lie on my side with my husband spooning behind me,” she tells SELF. (Another option experts previously recommended to SELF includes child’s pose, which can give you better control over the positioning of your back. Or, for pelvic pain, you can hop on top to adjust the depth of penetration and keep it shallow.).

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, Isma indicates she uses a wedged, foam pillow under her hips for extra support too. (Yes, there are specialized sex pillows that stay sturdy and don’t flatten out, helping you maintain the right angle without discomfort.) “It’s not as effortless or spontaneous as it used to be,” Isma admits, reflecting on how creating intimacy has changed throughout the years. “But we’ve learned our ways to make it work.”.

According to Dr. Nelson, it’s a common misconception that sex is only “good” when it includes penetration and ends in an orgasm. But expanding your definition—not by lowering your standards but by adjusting them—can keep intimacy exciting and realistic.

In a recent development, that might mean focusing on in-the-moment sensations over outcomes: slower pacing, more touch, less pressure to cum. “He genuinely loves going down on me,” Isma says of her husband, describing a nightly, pre-bed ritual that they have maintained almost every day for the past five years. “I don’t usually finish, and neither does he. It just feels amazing. We always look forward to it.”.

Martin has found something similar through practicing erotic massages. “At first I was intimidated, because you hear so much about the decline in libido, pain, lack of newness.” Now, Martin states, the slow buildup and warm oil rubbing throughout her erogenous zones is what she anticipates most.

While sex after 60 may not be the kind of stuff that makes it onto racy TV scenes (for now!), that’s precisely what experts say gives it power: It’s a slow, personalized intimacy built only through decades of experimentation, exploration, and curiosity—the kind that only gets better with age.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?

In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books.

I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of key theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims.

A New Study Reveals 3 Migraine Triggers That Might Be Making Your Headaches Worse—See Them Here

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week.
  • That’s the major takeaway from fresh research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.
  • If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from fresh research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

For the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

Sources indicate that during the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

The study also showed that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers said.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s crucial to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

According to recent reports, it’s important to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

According to recent reports, air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor claims.

Sources indicate that air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

In a recent development, then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil indicates. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”.

Dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil says. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Industry observers note that dr. Ghafoor says she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:.

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:.

Migraine triggers are personal, making it vital to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

If levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor indicates.

It has been revealed that when heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she says. “All of that is a very crucial part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”.

Ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very notable,” Dr. Ghafoor indicates. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”.

  • Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.
  • ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a fresh contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.

Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a fresh contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

In a recent development, “The design centres on a dialogue between old and newly introduced. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other,” studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.

“The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond,” he added.

“The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings.”.

A defining feature of the barn’s latest rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

In the ground floor’s flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.

Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn’s roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

According to recent reports, “The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond,” mentioned Edgley.

“Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame,” he added.

“The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project.”.

ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.

Previous projects by the studio include a terraced home in London with perforated metal floors to filter daylight and a green-terrazzo flat extension modelled on bay windows.

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

Industry observers note that I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. #137280. Working mothers face widespread discrimination in London’s commercial art world, report finds

Working mothers face widespread discrimination in London’s commercial art world, report finds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The contemporary art world has become increasingly adept at putting feminism, gender equality and the politics of care at the centre of its public-facing programming.
  • Not far at all, according to the first ever peer-reviewed study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published today by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance.
  • Recent findings suggest that based on a survey of 50 art world employees working across the UK capital’s galleries and auction houses, including 12 in-depth interviews, research by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The contemporary art world has become increasingly adept at putting feminism, gender equality and the politics of care at the centre of its public-facing programming. Galleries mount exhibitions exploring women's experiences, champion female artists and engage with questions of representation and social justice. But how far do those values extend to the women working behind the scenes?

Not far at all, according to the first ever peer-reviewed study on motherhood and discrimination in London’s commercial art world, published today by the European Journal of Cultural Studies and The Art Working Parents Alliance.

Recent findings suggest that based on a survey of 50 art world employees working across the UK capital’s galleries and auction houses, including 12 in-depth interviews, research by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi exposes a workplace culture in which mothering children often comes at considerable professional cost. As the report puts it: “Becoming a parent is at the root of the glass ceiling, and for many, it represents the glass cliff.”.

Three-quarters of survey respondents say becoming a parent has negatively affected their career progression, while more than one in five say they had been explicitly denied promotion. One woman was told she was ineligible for promotion while on maternity leave—a breach of UK law. Just 54% received enhanced maternity pay, compared with a national workplace average of 74.1%.

And these problems are not limited to smaller companies. “We assumed this would affect small art galleries with between five and 20 staff, but we found that big, multi-national galleries are also failing,” McMillan indicates. As the report notes: “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”.

According to recent reports, roberts-Komireddi believes that the “culture of secrecy” that enshrouds much of the art market—where financial transactions, benefits and networks are opaque and rarely disclosed—contributes to the discrimination women face when they become mothers. “Opacity really serves certain individuals and maintains this sense of fear, which was something I found particularly startling when we did our 12 in-depth interviews,” she indicates. “Fear and perceived retribution pervade these workplaces and women’s relationships to these workplaces.”.

That fear is often felt as soon as women announce their pregnancies. The report documents, among other instances, a pregnant woman being made redundant while experiencing a high-risk pregnancy, an employer attempting to dissolve a pregnant employee’s role and use the money to hire a newly introduced salesperson and a woman who miscarried returning to her desk immediately after a hospital appointment because she feared taking time off would damage her career. One interviewee describes feeling that by becoming pregnant she was making herself “vulnerable and less valuable”.

The findings also point to a deeper contradiction within an industry that publicly champions equality but often operates according to an unforgiving model of constant availability, international travel and after-hours networking. The art critic and curator Hettie Judah, who is a co-founder of The Art Working Parents Alliance, describes the colliding of 6pm private views with bedtime routines as the “witching hour” clash.

In a recent development, the difficulties are not confined to maternity leave itself. For many, the return to work can prove more damaging. Interviewees describe coming back to find their responsibilities have been redistributed, their relationships with artists and clients disrupted, or their standing within the gallery diminished. One woman discovered that a colleague who had covered her maternity leave had been given half her role, along with the artists she had spent years representing. Another returned from leave to find there was no desk for her in the gallery’s latest office.

Industry observers note that crucially, the report reveals the lack of formal HR structures across the commercial art sector. Only half of the respondents worked for galleries with dedicated HR staff, while just 30 of the 50 stated their workplace had a specific maternity or parental leave policy. In some cases, employees were left to research their own entitlements, negotiate their packages and even draft policies themselves. The report’s authors say that a lack of professional HR expertise contributed to instances of discriminatory practice and breaches of the UK Equality Act.

Sources indicate that the consequences can be far-reaching. For many women, the choice has been stark: find a way to accommodate the demands of motherhood or compromise their careers. Three-quarters of the women interviewed made changes to their careers after becoming pregnant, with some moving into freelance or independent work, taking less senior positions or leaving the industry altogether. Only a third of survey respondents were offered flexible working on their return, while half were expected to be in the office four or five days a week. One interviewee described the culture as one in which “presentism is more important than doing the work”.

The role of class and wealth is key in shaping these experiences. The report notes how some senior figures have access to live-in nannies, au pairs and domestic help, leaving them less attuned to the financial and practical pressures facing employees who must balance childcare with demanding working hours. One interviewee stated that the management team “all had night nurses, and you know, people helping at night. So, for them to understand that you’d had three hours of interrupted sleep and were expected to be at an opening, and a dinner, get home at 12:30 and then get up at 4:30 again, was impossible”.

Recent findings suggest that for those on more modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make evening events and travel particularly difficult to sustain. The report suggests that the more junior and precarious the employee, the greater the likelihood of experiencing discrimination—and the fewer resources they have to challenge it.

These divisions are not simply a question of wealth, however. They also complicate assumptions about gender solidarity within an industry where women make up a significant proportion of the workforce, but senior positions are often occupied by men. As Roberts-Komireddi points out, the assumption that women will necessarily support other women can be misleading—some of the more surprising testimonies in the report describe male directors showing greater sympathy towards pregnant employees than their female counterparts.

It has been revealed that these accounts suggest that the treatment of working mothers is shaped not simply by the gender of those in positions of authority, but by a wider workplace culture in which employees have little power to challenge established practices. Indeed, the report argues that discriminatory treatment is widespread, identifying breaches of the Equality Act in the experiences of all the women interviewed. Yet legal cases rarely make it to an employment tribunal. “In the UK, up until 1 October this year, women only had three months to bring a case to tribunal, which is not a lot of time, particularly if you’re about to give birth,” Roberts-Komireddi notes. “There’s a reluctance to go down that route because it’s a long, tiring, expensive process.”.

Sources indicate that looking ahead, the report’s authors hope to set best practice in the art industry. “If you look at huge corporations like Google, they have changed their policies in order to retain and attract mothers who make excellent staff—we could learn a lot from them,” Roberts-Komireddi states.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” mentioned Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

It has been revealed that “It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”.

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” noted Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Customers shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”.

GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

#137278. After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal.
  • At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy.
  • If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that during my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

As the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

In a recent development, that is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

Recent findings suggest that the data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Sources indicate that research reveals that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

Industry observers note that in my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

That matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

The lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Recent findings suggest that black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

In a recent development, it’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt.
  • Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project.
  • Sources indicate that “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AUBURN, Alabama — In Lowndes County, Alabama, less than an hour from Gee’s Bend, a group of women meet weekly to quilt together in a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church. In 2021, they began to carefully stitch the names of formerly enslaved congregation members into their work. What started as a project to preserve and commemorate these forgotten figures of history soon grew into a broader collaboration across Alabama.

Sew Their Names: Quilting, Creativity, and Activism at the Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art at Auburn University culminates a three-year partnership between the university and the Hopewell Project. The exhibition showcases a series of handmade quilts by Yvonne Wells, Wini McQueen, and Mercedes Braxton, alongside fellow Lowndes County artists including Bill Traylor, Noah Purifoy, and Charlie Lucas, highlighting the region's rich artistic tradition.

Sources indicate that “A lot of the time, when institutions are trying to connect with communities, they’re parachuting artists into a place that already has art and culture there,” Randi Evans, the former Manager of Public Practice and Community Partnerships at the Museum, explains. “We were really cognizant of our role, to work away from that narrative and work in collaboration with what was already happening at these sites.”.

A transplant herself, Evans hoped to learn about the traditions of Southern artists when she attended the quilt symposium “Every Stitch a Story,” hosted on Auburn’s campus. After Evans heard about the “Sew Their Names” project through a presentation by Judge Susan Walker, she thought it might be a good fit for the Museum in Motion initiative at the Jule. Previously, this initiative supported the 2022 exhibition Spell, Time, Practice, American, Body: The Work of RaMell Ross; Evans herself spearheaded partnerships across Hale County, where Ross’s film Hale County This Morning, This Evening (2018) was made.

Workshops at Auburn University's Rural Studio, November 2024 (both photos Mike Cortez).

“Since Auburn is a land grant institution, we see that part of our mission is taking the museum beyond our walls and reaching out to other parts of the state,” says Christy Barlow, the Museum’s Assistant Director of Education, Engagement, and Learning. Supported by resources from the Jule, “Sew Their Names” traveled around the state, pairing a showcase of quilts by commissioned artists with a series of workshops that allowed community members to participate in the quilt-making process.

It has been revealed that the first workshop took place in November 2024, as the exhibition traveled to Hale County, where Auburn’s Rural Studio, an off-campus architecture program focused on rural housing development, is located. The quilts were exhibited at a variety of local venues — what Evans termed a “quilt trail” — including Newbern Library, a project by Rural Studio; Sumac Cottage, an art gallery in Greensboro; and the Safe House Black History Museum, which foregrounded the exhibition’s focus on historical reckoning.

The exhibition then traveled to the Project Threadways Symposium in Florence, Alabama. Founded by designer and textile artist Natalie Chanin, the symposium’s 2025 edition focused on food, clothing, and shelter. The symposium also hosted a quilt-making workshop at the Kennedy-Douglass Center for the Arts in Florence. “Part of the experience of the Mt. Willing quilters is that they also sing as they work,” explains Barlow, who attended many of the in-person workshops. “So the singing is happening, and you have people scattered all throughout this historic house, sewing, learning to sew, learning about this story.”.

By early 2026, the exhibition made its way back to the Jule for a more permanent place in the main gallery; as Barlow explains, this is an unusual trajectory for a curatorial project. “Most of the time, the curatorial side develops an exhibition, and then education responds to it,” she notes. “However, this was a Museum in Motion initiative which eventually led to an exhibition. When you work that way, you have more input from community voices, who are part of the conversation from the very beginning.”.

Within the exhibition gallery, alongside featured quilts by Wini McQueen, Yvonne Wells, and Mercedes Braxton, other work by fellow Lowndes County natives was showcased. This included a painting by internationally renowned outsider artist Bill Traylor, a vivid three-dimensional collage by Noah Purifoy, a sculpture by Charlie Lucas, and a poster from the Lowndes County Freedom Organization. By pairing works from their permanent collection alongside quilts by the community, the exhibition emphasizes not only the variety of artistic forms across the region, but also the overt political nature of these practices; the Lowndes County Freedom Organization, for example, fought to empower Black voters during a time of extreme violence and intimidation.

According to recent reports, the exhibition soon became a focus of class visits from across Auburn University, drawing students in art history, philosophy, history, and even engineering. “A lot of Alabama-born students may not have a museum in their community,” explains Charlotte Hendrix, the museum’s communications director. “The Jule may be their first encounter walking into a space that can be intimidating; they might feel that they have to know a lot about art. When students participate in the process, you really can’t beat that, in terms of active, engaged learning.”.

Tech Report: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sources indicate that sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, claims Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

It has been revealed that the textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

It has been revealed that some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin claims.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Sources indicate that women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, states Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

Industry observers note that and it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin states. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

According to recent reports, home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin says. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

Sources indicate that that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

According to recent reports, if left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, claims Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra states, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

According to recent reports, because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition challenges and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research demonstrates that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that as researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s key to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

#137273. So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1673 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hyperallergic ↗ Open Full Page

So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades.
  • In a recent development, for example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle.
  • In a recent development, the following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Much has been written about the “Great Wealth Transfer,” a predicted $80+ trillion phenomenon that will enrich younger generations as their parents pass away in the next two decades. For those who have inherited — or expect to inherit — the estates of visual artists, the challenges of this “transfer” can be especially complex. Works of art, which can carry both emotional and sentimental value alongside asset value, require special care and consideration. The resulting pressures and responsibilities can divide families and create legal challenges.

In a recent development, for example, when the artist Sam Francis died in 1994, he left over 1,000 artworks, several businesses, extensive real estate holdings, ten cars, and a herd of cattle. His will provided money for a foundation called “The Sam Francis Museum,” but his vague instructions did not specify its activities. Disputes among his heirs — Francis had four children and had been married five times — and the need to extensively document his artwork further complicated matters. Settling all parties' claims and establishing the Sam Francis Foundation took nearly five years.

In a recent development, the following text, which touches on topics facing estates, was developed in consultation with experts in fields that serve estates and trustees. There are also many organizations doing vital work to advance this field, including the Center for the Preservation of Artists' Legacies, the Artists' Legacy Foundation, and Legacy Lab New Mexico.

Ideally, estate planning should begin while the artist is alive, with someone available to guide the process and provide key information. Record contact information for key associates, including dealers and others, along with instructions for working with them. The estate will need access to digital assets, including archives, email correspondence, and computer files. Setting up a revocable trust can help the estate avoid probate, allowing assets and property to pass swiftly to heirs, and also provides great privacy.

Industry observers note that when it comes to choosing trustees, Joe Oliveira, the sole trustee of the Nathan Oliveira Estate, said, “Choosing trustees can be difficult, and they may not necessarily be family members. In my own case, I happen to be the most logical candidate. A single trustee like myself can make decisions efficiently and consistently, while still listening to and considering the ideas of other family members.”.

Sources indicate that one of the most crucial challenges estate managers face is understanding and cataloging an estate’s full contents. This includes not only works of art but also related ephemera, such as correspondence and personal effects. Unique ephemera, like Joan Brown’s fingerprint-covered telephone on display at her SFMOMA retrospective, can strengthen future exhibition narratives.

Recent findings suggest that stuart A. Chase, a former museum director who now advises estates, suggests starting with an inventory. “In my experience, most heirs have no idea what they have. You can’t do anything without a catalog. You can’t approach anyone. It can be very simple: I use CatalogIt, which is straightforward to use and charges a nominal fee.”.

It has been revealed that when I took Chase’s advice and used CatalogIt to document my art collection, I looked under the bed and found a folder of unframed drawings a friend gave me years ago that I'd completely forgotten about. The app allowed me to print a copy of the completed inventory, which I added to my will.

In a recent development, an appraisal, an independent assessment of a property's value or condition, is essential to managing an artist’s estate because it involves the IRS. A Fair Market Value appraisal is typically required to file estate taxes and establish latest cost bases for each work in the event of future sales by an heir. It will contain detailed reports for each object, including artist, title, date, dimensions, medium, provenance, condition, and the specific valuation method used. The IRS requires what it calls “qualified appraisals” for this, as well as for non-cash charitable donations to qualified institutions and other gifts.

Choose appraisers carefully, and select those who are highly recommended. Deborah Gerstler Spanierman, a longtime art advisor and certified appraiser, recommends engaging “qualified and trustworthy allied professionals: appraisers, archivists, estate and foundation attorneys to handle the estate tax filing. Empower them to do their jobs and to work with the artist’s gallery, if they have one, which will all eventually support the artist’s legacy.”.

Artist-Endowed Foundations differ from other philanthropic measures because they create programs that feature the artist’s work. These may include organizing and lending to exhibitions, developing and publishing catalogue raisonnés, or operating education centers.

Christine Vincent, the managing director of the Aspen Institute, an artist-endowed foundation initiative, explains: “Artists' estates and Artist-Endowed Foundations (AEFs) are entirely different things. Artists' estates are typically operated by private individuals and, as such, are not tax-exempt charitable entities. AEFs are tax-exempt charitable organizations with a mission to benefit the general public. An artist's estate may evolve into an AEF, for example under the estate plan of an artist's surviving spouse, but an AEF can never devolve into an artist's estate.”.

Industry observers note that checking an artist’s archive for condition issues is essential. Identify which works need immediate care, which will need future restoration and/or repair, and act as promptly as possible. You might have to make difficult decisions about works that should be discarded or destroyed with the utmost consideration. Seek expert help — from conservators and other art professionals — when works require special treatment or present unique problems.

Sources indicate that where you store work also affects its condition. “Know how to properly store works on canvas and paper in temperature-controlled spaces, and insure them to avoid any future or potential loss,” claims Jamieson Grillo, the sole trustee of the Estate of John Grillo. “If the estate can afford it, make sure you get your artwork conserved by a professional conservator with past experience and a proven track record in conserving similar art. Also, share any conservation reports with galleries you are working with.”.

Galleries with long-term relationships with artists will likely want to continue that partnership after an artist passes away. But estates seeking new representation should start by identifying suitable galleries, looking at those that handle works similar to the estate’s.

Prioritize and prepare before contacting any galleries. Gallery owner Hollis Taggart swears by making it as easy as possible for the gallery by providing as much detail as possible. “The more organized an estate is, the more likely a gallery will be to take on the heavy lifting of representing that estate.” Taggart also advises a clear vision: “Be as supportive as possible by organizing an inventory list of the works so the gallery knows right up front what the estate holdings are, and how big a project is involved.”.

Placing works in museum collections helps enhance and maintain an artist’s reputation and legacy. But museums often hesitate to accept donations because of limited exhibition and storage space. Patti Smith, an art collections manager at the Stephenson Ceramics Studio, suggests approaching them thoughtfully and presenting only high-quality works, or collaborating with a gallery to develop a “gifting exhibition.” She states, “I helped develop one for the estate of artist Richard Wilt (1915–1981) that documented a body of his work and displayed it in the gallery. We approached new museums as well as museums that already had his work. Since there was demand for purchasing the work, once the museums made their selections, the work was offered up for sale, and 100% of the proceeds went to the Richard Wilt Foundation at the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art and Design.”.

Estates should have websites that include an artist biography, a timeline, a gallery of works, and contact information. This can help anyone doing research — including appraisers and dealers — and may also help locate lost works.

According to recent reports, A social media presence, especially regular Instagram posts, keeps an artist’s legacy in the public consciousness. Mary Clare McKinley of the Richard Diebenkorn Foundation indicates, “When estates and foundations harness the power of social media, it can be a brilliant tool for education, legacy and community building. In my opinion, investing in research is always a good decision. Then, consider the platform a way to share information less formally than publishing a book, and creatively explore ways to use it: Enjoy the flexibility, interactivity, and immediate access to a wider public.” She shares that the Diebenkorn Foundation’s Instagram posts “highlight scholars making exciting discoveries, support museum exhibitions, feature [their] own intriguing archival finds, and suggest new visual connections to Diebenkorn’s work.”.

According to the Center for Art Law, when an artist passes, their estate has two seemingly conflicting tasks: "to protect an artist’s work by exercising exclusive rights over them, and to disseminate their artwork to the public to establish a lasting legacy and placement in the art world.” But this dilemma runs parallel to another matter: Should estates prioritize revenue, or improve public access to art?

Auction results, now widely available through online databases, are key public indicators of an artist’s salability. Selling an especially strong work at auction is a gamble some estates take to establish a benchmark for an artist whose work lacks a previous auction record. Estates of recognized artists may want to partner with an auction house to mount a significant sale.

To do so, an estate needs to meet certain standards. Wendy Battleson, senior vice president at Bonhams, claims, “Auction houses, in general, are looking for an estate with an established record of sales at relatively high values (five to six figures minimum), ideally sold publicly. We also look at the amount of inventory available in order to continue to tell the artist’s story over a period of time. The beauty of working with an auction house is that pricing is public, and there is rarely a concern that the art has been sold for less than market rate. With a dealer, the sales are typically private, so you don’t know if you could have achieved a higher price.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Sunday, the Venice Biennale will award its new “Visitors’ Lions.” But no matter who receives this poisoned chalice, the results are void.

In a recent development, stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the upcoming Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most key biennial. After the jury publicly stated their intention to omit Israel and Russia from consideration for the Golden Lions, they were visited by representatives from Italy’s Ministry of Culture. The contents of the meeting are not public, but we can surmise how it went from the jury’s subsequent unanimous resignation. Shortly after, the Venice Biennale Foundation declared the Visitors’ Lions, inviting ticket-holders to cast their vote for awards to be announced at the end of the show’s run.

“Our exclusion has been thwarted, and the choice now passes to the general public,” crowed Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, whom human rights groups accuse of orchestrating the siege of Kamal Adwan Hospital and the notorious imprisonment and torture of the hospital’s director, Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, in 2024. Firmly siding with torture and against principle, the Biennale made it clear that both Israel and Russia were back in the running for the Visitors’ Lions. As Antonia Majaca observed, the jury dared to apply a criterion, and the Biennale responded by dissolving judgment itself.

Many artists have rejected this sham from the start. On the day the 2026 Biennale opened to the public, 54 artists in the international exhibition and 22 national pavilion teams withdrew from consideration in solidarity with the jury. In June, more than a hundred artists threatened legal action unless their names were removed from the ballot. Sunday’s ceremony awards a prize that few want to win.

In a recent development, the massive public pushback against the Biennale also demonstrates how close we have come to actualizing the moral principle that a genocidal, apartheid state has no legitimacy on any international stage. This year, we participated in a series of unprecedented protests. Biennale artists and cultural workers went on strike three times in seven months — nothing on this scale has ever happened before (not even during the anti-capitalist protests of 1968, which put a stop to the Biennale’s prizes for 18 years). This year’s protests were also unprecedented in terms of the level of collaboration between ANGA — which comprises artists, curators, and precariously employed workers — and rank-and-file labor unions.

The Biennale is resolutely global, unfolding in the “anywhere or not at all” of the international art circuit. Against the false globalization of the art market, our internationalism was grounded in local organizing against Israel’s Zionist genocide.

Industry observers note that the first of this year’s strikes, on May 8, was built locally in Venice, with Biennalocene, Sale Docks, and other local grassroots unions whose participation provided legal protection for striking art workers. On May 8, 30 of the Biennale’s 100 national pavilions closed partially or fully, and thousands of people marched from Via Garibaldi to the Arsenale, where they were met with police brutality. Many artists in the main exhibition draped or altered their works.

The second strike, on June 12, was national in scale. It was the result of a year of organizing assemblies and actions in about 20 cities all around Italy, with organizations including Mi Riconosci?, Vogliamo Tutt’Altro, Biennalocene, and grassroots unions through the Cultural Strike platform.

It has been revealed that the third strike, on 30 October, responded to a call that emerged from outside the art world from the World Federation of Trade Unions and, in Italy, was taken up by militant dockworkers, including the Autonomous Collective of Port Workers, and the grassroots Unione Sindacale di Base. A network of port unions at 113 in 22 countries, including Italy, France, Greece, Turkey, and Morocco, refused to load weapons bound for Israel. This was the biggest ever coordinated action of its kind, and our role was to help build local participation in Venice.

Today, November 20, as this piece is being published, the International Student Strike brought further strike action to Venice, demonstrating the political convergence between students and the Biennale — students in the city are often employed in the cultural sector under precarious conditions.

In a recent development, our ability to do this grew out of the work we began in 2024, in adherence to the guidelines of the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) and Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS), when our open letter demanding Israel’s exclusion from the Biennale was signed by more than 24,000 cultural workers. That year, the Israel pavilion closed.

Sources indicate that between 2024 and 2026, our campaign connected more substantively with the Italian labor movement. As the June 12 strike articulated, the political atomization of artists is a labor matter, related to the art world’s reliance on precarity, which shifts the risk of political action onto individuals. The Biennale provides no fees or production money to artists, leaving them to fundraise their participation. Those whose work is not sufficiently market-friendly to claw back payment in future sales have to content themselves with being paid in the false currency of prestige.

ANGA refuses the oppressive logic that allows the Biennale to support genocide and profit from precarious labor while claiming to rise above politics. This year, we have made clear that the alliance we have created has the power to disrupt the Biennale’s functioning and change its nature.

Today, the contradictions of the present political order — the indigestible, white-supremacy-coded cocktail of Europe’s simultaneous opposition to Russia and support for Israel; the flailing, ever-dying economy; the oceans of money poured into technologies of death and destruction — explode messily into the supposedly morally hermetic market-world of the Biennale.

Recent findings suggest that the farcical “Visitors’ Lions” are the Biennale’s wager that the walls can always be painted pure white again. But this year’s massive actions have demonstrated that we will not allow Israel’s unspeakable assault on Palestine to be art-washed and ignored. ANGA’s members and supporters are no less steadfast than we were three years ago, when our campaign first began. It remains obvious and undeniable that Israel, the United States-backed abattoir-state, must not be allowed to bring its logic of butchery to be art-washed into neutral “complexity” at the Biennale. And we are now considerably more organized and better connected to the wider struggle against Zionism.

Sources indicate that when we look back to ANGA’s beginnings, in early 2024, we remember a time when the shock of total Zionist impunity was still raw enough to feel unreal. We could not imagine that friends or colleagues could disagree with this basic principle. We were soon disabused, as many cultural workers washed their hands of blood in service of their careers.

Sources indicate that but our collective efforts have transformed this anti-political status quo. The latest compositions of struggle made possible by the mass revolt against Zionism offer a model for how the art world can reach beyond the isolated precarity of cultural labor into new alliances — with students, with dockworkers. The power of boycott as a tool has never been greater. We continue to remake the Venice Biennale, the modern world exhibition, from Walter Benjamin’s “place of pilgrimage to the commodity fetish” into a site of struggle.

#137270. In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism
